item.title: Clashes Darken Rally in South Carolina as Trump Seeks to Boost Darline Graham
item.description:
More than half a dozen clashes between rallygoers and protesters interrupted President Trump at an appearance in Clemson, S.C., on Wednesday night, where he had traveled to boost the campaign of Senator Darline Graham.

It was not the first Trump rally in recent days marred by protests. But the drumbeat of outbursts, followed by angry reactions by the president and his supporters, showed the deep political divide in the country as the Nov. 3 elections draw near.

Mr. Trump is in the midst of a six-day barnstorm across some the country’s most conservative states, seeking to shore up support among his fans at a time when Republicans are increasingly pessimistic about whether they can retain control of Congress.

South Carolina is among a raft of traditionally Republican strongholds that have become battlegrounds this cycle. Polling in these places shows that Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries for everyday Americans — have threatened the party’s fortunes.

The clashes on Wednesday between protesters, who interrupted Mr. Trump with screams and expletives, and rallygoers who responded with similar aggression, underscored how much is at stake in these midterms for a deeply polarized electorate.

One after the next, security officers escorted the protesters out of the arena, while the president’s fans whooped, jeered and chanted “U.S.A.” Mr. Trump did little to de-escalate the atmosphere.

“They’re terrible people,” he said after hearing one disruption.

“Who’s that guy who threw a punch?” he asked after another, appearing to celebrate when a rallygoer physically confronted a demonstrator.

Mr. Trump had traveled to this livestock facility in the northwest corner of South Carolina to help Ms. Graham at a time when polls show her in an unexpectedly tight race against her Democratic opponent, Dr. Annie Andrews.

The South Carolina governor, Henry McMaster, appointed Ms. Graham over the summer to fill out the remainder of the term of her brother, Senator Lindsey Graham, who died in July. The president then endorsed her for a full six-year term.

His choice of Ms. Graham, who had no prior political experience, in a tough political environment for Republicans has forced the party to pour resources into defending a seat in a state Mr. Trump carried in 2024 by more than 17 points.

On Tuesday, the Cook Political Report shifted the Senate race toward Dr. Andrews for the second time in less than a month, this time from Likely Republican to Lean Republican.

The rally showed signs of helping Ms. Graham, who needs to varnish her conservative credentials in a region called the Upstate, where ultraconservative voters were known to be critical of her brother for what they viewed as his soft stance on immigration and history of compromising with Democrats.

Mr. Trump drew a full house to the facility, and the crowd whooped and hollered at his punchlines on immigration and the media with energy reminiscent of his rallies in prior cycles. He invited Ms. Graham, who had spoken earlier in the evening, to join him onstage.

“This area, and most importantly its values, are ingrained in me,” said Ms. Graham, who was raised in the Upstate. “God, family, country.”

Earlier in the night, Senator Tim Scott and Representative Russell Fry, who ran against Ms. Graham in a bitterly fought primary election, vouched for her conservative bona fides.

Mr. Trump’s extensive efforts on behalf of Ms. Graham helped her win the primary election, but not without avoiding a runoff election against Representative Ralph Norman, the vice chair of the hard-line Freedom Caucus. Counties in the Upstate broke for Mr. Norman, who has been at best a reluctant supporter of Ms. Graham’s general election candidacy.

On a podcast episode that aired on Wednesday, Mr. Norman said he would vote for Ms. Graham, but his family would not. Mr. Norman also said he would not do any events with his former opponent — a promise he appeared to keep on Wednesday, when he was nowhere to be found at Clemson.

Mr. Trump spoke for about an hour and a half. At one point, he said he was in a “good mood.” At other moments, he looked into the crowd and saw men with their middle fingers in the air, then watched as security officers escorted them from the hall.

item.title: Judge Restricts D.H.S. Field Operations Aimed at Unearthing Voter Fraud
item.description:
A federal judge in California on Wednesday blocked the Homeland Security Department from carrying out most field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in nine states as part of a broader push to identify noncitizen voters.

The ruling came less than two weeks before the midterm elections. The Trump administration has launched a blitz of operations focused on finding evidence of noncitizen voting or tying up election processes in states where it has dubiously claimed that large numbers of noncitizens are registered to vote.

The ruling covered stops and field interviews being carried out by hundreds of Department of Homeland Security agents assigned to fan out across the country in search of instances of voter fraud, under what the administration has referred to as the “Unlawful Voter Initiative.”

In a concise 19-page ruling, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin wrote that the stops appeared likely to hamper voter engagement and registration by a coalition of local governments and nonprofit groups. As with other initiatives in which the Trump administration has used federal immigration data to infer the citizenship status of people on state voter rolls, she wrote there were already signs that the “target lists” the government had generated contained errors and included naturalized citizens.

The Department of Homeland Security has defended its methods, saying federal officials had used multiple data sources in addition to the public voter data they pulled to further verify the identity of registrants and eliminate false positives.

Judge Martínez-Olguin stopped short of halting field operations. But she barred agents from carrying out interviews that “involve or are likely to involve persons” who agents “know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens.” Given the unreliability of federal citizenship data at issue in the case, it was unclear how significantly that would hamper the department’s activities.

The interests of the entities suing, “and the public’s interest in safe elections, free from interference or intimidation,” she wrote, “far exceed defendants’ purported interest in combating unlawful voting by non-U.S. citizens.”

Internal documents introduced in the case indicated that agents were directed to focus on California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.

Judge Martínez-Olguin, who was appointed by President Joseph R. Biden Jr., wrote that the scope of the operations also raised concerns about voter intimidation. She noted that according to agency memos, the Homeland Security Department “surveils, covertly infiltrates and interrogates the staff of nonprofits and churches conducting voter engagement” and had targeted nearly 150 such nonprofit groupsas of July.

The government had indicated it could target naturalized citizens in instances where data suggested an individual had voted before they were naturalized.

The case arose as the Trump administration has mounted a series of legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections. The efforts have been largely unsuccessful, in part because many of the state and local authorities that administer and supervise elections have refused to comply with demands for access to sensitive voter rolls.

As a result, the federal authorities have compiled their own databases, underpinned by public, commercially available information that they have compared with federal records. The process has led to mistakes in some states, in part because public voter rolls do not include unique identifiers like Social Security numbers. Federal immigration records also sometimes fail to capture changes in citizenship status.

Election authorities in Los Angeles said the Justice Department’s lists of suspected noncitizen voters were so sloppily compiled that they seemed almost “performative” in nature, with thousands of names lacking Social Security numbers and other crucial identifying information. Many of the names, they said, were paired with addresses over which Los Angeles had no jurisdiction.

A spokesman for the Los Angeles County registrar’s office said the list was initially sent on a thumb drive that was unusable because it posed a risk to sensitive voter information, and called the federal demand “a data dump.”

Judge Martínez-Olguin paused her order from taking effect until Friday evening, allowing the government time to appeal. She wrote that order would lift at the end of Election Day, on Nov. 3, “or as otherwise directed by the court.”

It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections, and decades of evidence show that instances of noncitizen voting are exceptionally rare in the United States, far beneath levels that the administration alleges. Scrutiny of claims by the administration that large numbers of noncitizens voted in states like Nevada, for example, have caused the allegations to collapse.

The Homeland Security Department’s operations aimed at finding verified cases of voter fraud comes as the Trump administration has mounted a series of escalating — and largely unsuccessful — legal fights with election officials across the country, aiming to show a pattern of large-scale illegal voting in U.S. elections.

The administration has particularly singled out states led by Democrats like California, where officials have refused to comply with demands for access to voter rolls. Last week, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles gave local election officials 48 hours to verify the citizenship or segregate the ballots of 20,000 people on a list of potential noncitizens they said had been compiled by the Homeland Security Department.

When California officials said that timeline was impossible to comply with, the Department of Justice filed suit to prevent any ballots sent to those people from being counted.

On Monday, the federal authorities announced they had released from custody 28 immigrants throughout the state who they said were suspected of registering to vote or voting in California elections before becoming naturalized citizens. All had green cards and many denied ever knowingly registering or voting. The group represented a tiny fraction — roughly one in a million — of the roughly 23 million registered voters in the state.

item.title: Farmers, Health Care and Highways: 5 Takeaways from the Kansas Senate Debate
item.description:
Once upon a time, the Kansas Senate race was expected to be a sleepy affair, one where Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican, would cruise to re-election.

Then came Adam Hamilton.

In a matter of months, Mr. Hamilton, the Democratic nominee, has turned the deep red state into one of the most unexpected battlegrounds of the midterms, putting Mr. Marshall on the defensive in a contentious campaign that has pumped the airwaves full of attack ads.

So the most surprising thing about Wednesday night’s Senate debate might just have been how civil it was.

The moderator, John Holt of Fox4 in Kansas City, skillfully dispensed with the main attacks of the campaign in its opening minutes and pushed the two men instead to tangle over substance. They stuck to his rules and — no doubt unintentionally — even presented a unified sartorial front, wearing matching dark suits and silvery ties.

And both candidates tried to use their time onstage to transform the race into a referendum on unpopular national figures: President Trump and Senator Chuck Schumer, the Democratic leader.

Here are five takeaways from the night.

No one has more practice at extemporaneous talking than a megachurch pastor.

Mr. Hamilton, who founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the nation’s largest United Methodist congregation, is comfortable delivering sermons and speaking on long podcasts. That showed, as he deftly navigated a lightning-speed debate that veered from foreign policy to farming to artificial intelligence, creating a stark contrast with Mr. Marshall, who spoke haltingly and sometimes tripped over his words.

Mr. Hamilton blamed Mr. Marshall for what he framed as the excesses of the Trump administration — including record diesel prices and immigration raids in farm country — while seeking to present himself as an independent-minded Democrat who has steered clear of his own party’s more extreme positions.

He spoke sparingly about his faith, but used his status as a political newcomer to separate himself from the national party, as when Mr. Marshall sought to connect him to former President Barack Obama’s immigration policies.

“You were pointing at me as though I developed these policies,” Mr. Hamilton said. “I just want to remind you, I’ve been a pastor for the last 38 years. I have not been a senator. I didn’t develop policies with President Obama or anyone else.”

Mr. Holt, the moderator, lobbed detailed questions at the candidates and pressed repeatedly when they tried to sidestep them. At times, Mr. Hamilton answered with candor: He just wasn’t sure.

At one point, Mr. Holt asked both candidates where, exactly, they would draw the line on subsidies for farmers — a delicate question in a year when farmers are facing strong economic headwinds, some of which have been exacerbated by the Trump administration.

Mr. Marshall defended the subsidies.

Mr. Hamilton, who has said on the campaign trail that he doesn’t want to come up with “bogus” answers, said: “I don’t really have an answer to that. I can only say this: that we do need to be able to help our farmers. Our farmers need support.”

He said he would raise the cap on Social Security, but he wasn’t sure to what level. And he said he wasn’t sure what federal regulations he would support on artificial intelligence, in part because, he said, no one in Congress fully understands its dangers.

Mr. Marshall moved to highlight Mr. Hamilton’s inexperience, including once after an exchange over Israel — a country Mr. Hamilton said he had visited 12 times.

For “a novice even to start making national security policy without all the details, I think it’s really hard to do that,” Mr. Marshall said.

Republican candidates running in more traditional battleground states have attempted to distance themselves from President Trump and his unpopular policies, including the Iran war and tariffs. But not Mr. Marshall.

The senator offered a vocal defense of the president, saying he had fulfilled some of his central promises to voters. Mr. Trump, said Mr. Marshall, had strengthened the nation’s military, secured the borders and passed a sweeping tax cut.

His comments were part of an effort to remind Republican voters, including those frustrated by high gas prices and inflation, what they liked about the president. “If you want the Trump agenda to continue,” he said. “you need to come out, because we delivered on those things.”

Two years ago, Mr. Trump won Kansas by 16 points. To win this year, Mr. Marshall must persuade those voters to stick with Republicans, rather than stay home or cross party lines and vote for Mr. Hamilton.

“We need the Trump voters to come out,” he said.

With Mr. Trump facing record low approval ratings, Mr. Marshall attempted to energize Kansas Republicans by reminding them of a figure they like even less: Senator Chuck Schumer of New York, the Democratic leader in the Senate.

Again and again, Mr. Marshall warned that electing Mr. Hamilton would award control of the Senate to Democrats and Mr. Schumer. “This guy’s funded by Chuck Schumer,” he said. “He’ll be beholden to Chuck Schumer forever, and that’s why we have to keep me in that Senate seat.”

The repeated invocation of Mr. Schumer’s name was part of an effort by Mr. Marshall to nationalize the race, turning it into a referendum — not on Mr. Trump but on which party controls the Senate. While Mr. Trump is unpopular, Democrats also have plenty of detractors in this red state.

Mr. Hamilton has said he would not support Mr. Schumer as the head of the party in the Senate, arguing that Democrats need fresh leadership. In the debate, he tried to distance himself from national Democrats, calling former President Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s immigration policy a “disaster” and saying he does not agree with the “socialist party.”

“If I’m elected, as a moderate or independent-minded Democrat, I’m going to work across the aisle,” he said.

As the Kansas Senate race has grown more competitive, it has also become far more contentious.

The debate opened with both candidates being pressed on issues on which they have faced personal criticism. Mr. Marshall defended his aggressive debt collection practices as an obstetrician-gynecologist. Mr. Hamilton attempted to distance himself from an incident of child sex abuse at a church retreat two decades ago.

But they were also pressed on a range of substantive policy questions, including weapons support for Israel, immigration reform and health insurance. Mr. Hamilton hammered Mr. Marshall for backing unpopular policies of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran and tariffs.

For his part, Mr. Marshall attempted to link his opponent to unpopular positions held by some in his party, including support for trans girls playing women’s sports. (Mr. Hamilton said he would not want his 12-year-old granddaughter competing against biological men or boys, saying, “it’s not a fair fight.”)

But not every question was quite as serious.

In a Kansas twist, the moderator asked each candidate to select his favorite stretch of highway in the state.

Mr. Marshall chose Interstate 77 between Manhattan and Cassoday. Mr. Hamilton chose Interstate 35 through the Flint Hills. “One of the most beautiful places on God’s green earth,” he said.

item.title: 4 Takeaways From the Debate for Wisconsin Governor
item.description:
Representative Tom Tiffany of Wisconsin and David Crowley, the Milwaukee County executive, faced off on Wednesday over taxes, abortion and the influence of billionaires in a televised debate, their first and only one before the November election.

In Wisconsin, where statewide races are often decided by razor-thin margins, the debate was a crucial opportunity for Mr. Crowley to introduce himself to voters and for Mr. Tiffany to woo independents hesitant about his close ties with President Trump.

Polls show the candidates in a tight race less than two weeks from Election Day. Democrats hope to keep the governor’s mansion in their party’s hands — and possibly flip control of both the State Senate and the Assembly from Republicans to Democrats.

Here are four takeaways from Wednesday night’s debate, which was held at Marquette University in Milwaukee and hosted by a local news station, WISN 12.

Early in the debate, Mr. Tiffany, who was endorsed by President Trump, did not directly answer when asked how voters could trust him to represent their interests when he is so closely aligned with the president.

Mr. Tiffany is one of the most conservative members of Congress, known for his strong support for gun rights and lowering taxes and his opposition to using taxpayer money for abortions.

“As a lifelong resident, I will make sure that we are going to do what’s right for Wisconsin,” Mr. Tiffany said, before pivoting to wish his wife a happy anniversary and reminiscing about their first date at the Thirsty Whale, a restaurant in Minocqua, Wis.

He did not mention Mr. Trump.

But Mr. Crowley did — frequently. He said that Mr. Tiffany was part of the Trump agenda in Washington, which he said includes tariffs, “endless wars” and high gas prices.

The candidates sparred over how to improve the economy and bring in more revenue to Wisconsin, where families have pointed to affordability as one of the issues driving the governor’s race.

Mr. Tiffany said that he would support building more data centers under certain conditions: no more state subsidies, no increase in utility rates and a requirement that local communities be included in the decision-making process. He also insisted that no data centers be built “on our beautiful farmland here in Wisconsin,” a stipulation that seemed to open the door for building on former industrial sites.

Mr. Crowley, whom Mr. Tiffany has called “Data Center David” on the campaign trial, said that he supports a “pause” in data centers so that their environmental impact can be considered.

Both candidates were enthusiastic about legalizing marijuana — but with conditions.

Wisconsin, where marijuana is illegal, is now an outlier in the region. That has not stopped Wisconsin residents from driving into Minnesota, Michigan and Illinois and buying it in those states.

While Mr. Tiffany said he favored legalizing medical marijuana, Mr. Crowley said he supported full legalization of recreational sales as well.

“This is an opportunity that we’re missing out on as a state,” he said. Making a reference to Gov. J.B. Pritzker of neighboring Illinois, he added: “Look, Governor Pritzker literally thanked Wisconsin residents because they have made $30 million in sales tax collection just from Wisconsin residents.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Crowley has tried to draw attention to his support for abortion rights, in contrast to Mr. Tiffany, who has cosponsored a bill in Congress that would ban abortion after about six weeks of pregnancy.

Wisconsin currently bans abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy and requires an ultrasound and a 24-hour waiting period before an abortion can be performed. About two-thirds of Wisconsin residents say that abortion should be legal in most or all cases, polls show.

On Wednesday, Mr. Crowley dodged the question when asked if he would sign a law that would expand access to abortion with no limits.

“These are decisions that need to be made between a patient and a health care provider,” he said.

Mr. Tiffany said that he had listened to feedback from constituents on the campaign trail who had urged him to find a “common ground.” In response to a question from the moderators, he said he would not sign a hypothetical bill that would ban abortion after fetal cardiac activity could be detected.

Wisconsin is not overflowing with billionaires. But Mr. Crowley did his best to tie them to Mr. Tiffany, part of a continued line of attack connecting Mr. Tiffany to the rich and powerful in Washington.

“He’s working for the billionaires,” Mr. Crowley said. “He’s going to do anything and everything that they tell him to do because that’s who he’s been in the pockets of.”

At one point, Mr. Tiffany seemed fed up with the word.

“He’s misrepresenting our positions, and he’s over there ranting constantly about billionaires,” he said.

For his part, Mr. Tiffany tried to fuse Mr. Crowley’s positions as a Democrat with those of the opponent he defeated in the primary, Francesca Hong, who is a democratic socialist.

“He said, ‘There’s very little difference between me and Francesca Hong,’” he said. “That sounds like a socialist to me.”

Despite repeated pressing by the moderators, Matt Smith and Gerron Jordan, both candidates avoided specifics about how much they would raise or lower property and income taxes and how they would balance the state budget while also fulfilling pledges to make life more affordable for Wisconsin residents.

item.title: James Talarico Made His Name Fighting Republicans. He Made Laws With Them, Too.
item.description:
James Talarico’s record in the Texas Legislature has been a tale of two Talaricos.

There’s the Talarico who flipped a competitive state house district around Austin and arrived in the Capitol in 2019 as a 29-year-old, a Democrat preaching bipartisan cooperation. There, he accomplished things by working with Republicans, including 39 bills that became law with his name on them.

Then there’s the Talarico who was a vocal progressive fighter, especially after Republicans redrew his district lines, pushing him to run in a liberal Austin area. Voters there cheered as he fought unsuccessfully against religion in public schools and in favor of transgender rights.

The first Talarico earned accolades even from some of his Republican colleagues in the Legislature they dominate. The second, which helped catapult him into the national spotlight, is being used against him in his run for U.S. Senate.

Mr. Talarico has tried to balance his two political identities throughout his four terms in the Texas House, according to a New York Times review of his record and interviews with more than a dozen current and former legislators. Even as he worked against partisan bills pushed by the Legislature’s conservative majority, the review found his ability to work with Republicans to pass laws stayed largely consistent.

In his Senate campaign this year, Mr. Talarico has emphasized the bipartisan side of his record. Seeking to prevail in a state that President Trump won by nearly 14 points in 2024, he has toned down his criticism of Republicans and distanced himself from some past remarks, saying they “missed the mark” or were “cringe-y.”

His campaign literature no longer refers to him as a progressive.

“I worked with both Republicans and Democrats who wanted to get things done for Texans,” Mr. Talarico said in a statement. His campaign provided written answers but did not make him available for an interview.

In interviews with more than a dozen current and former legislators, Mr. Talarico was described as a driven and disciplined lawmaker who used his oratory skills to amplify the message of his party.

This week on “The Daily,” The Times’s podcast, Mr. Talarico said Republicans in the Legislature forced him into a position when he “had to fight back against that extremism.” He said his viewpoint on partisan politics has changed.

“When I first ran for office, I thought of it as left versus right,” he said. “I’ve now come to see politics as not left versus right but top versus bottom.”

Mr. Talarico has led his opponent, attorney general of Texas Ken Paxton, in nearly every recent poll, including with many independents. But to succeed on Election Day, he must win over at least some Republicans. To reach those voters, he has pointed to his record in office.

Madison Cercy, a spokeswoman for Mr. Paxton’s campaign, rejected the suggestion that Mr. Talarico had a record of bipartisanship.

“Now that he needs Texas voters, he’s scrubbing his website and pretending to be a moderate,” Ms. Cercy said. “Calling a radical a moderate isn’t a fair reading of his record.”

In one of his first speeches to the Texas House, Mr. Talarico urged lawmakers to put party aside.

“This next session shouldn’t be about the Democratic Party or the Republican Party,” Mr. Talarico said in 2019, weeks after winning election. “It should be about chasing a vision of what this state can be.”

During his nearly seven years in office, Mr. Talarico’s name appeared on more than 500 bills. More than three-quarters of the bills he wrote with other lawmakers had at least one Republican author or sponsor.

As a lead author, he passed laws to cap prekindergarten class size and help inmates earn high school diplomas. After a man died during the filming of a television show, he worked with Republicans to prohibit police departments from entering into reality TV agreements.

As with most Democratic bills in the Republican-controlled Legislature, his progressive measures largely went nowhere. He championed bills requiring diversity officers in public schools, legalizing marijuana and addressing climate change.

Few aspects of Mr. Talarico’s legislative record have proved as contentious as his positions and remarks on transgender issues, which Republicans have made a prominent line of attack.

Mr. Talarico — and nearly every other Democrat in the Legislature — unsuccessfully opposed bills restricting transgender athletes’ participation in youth and college sports. He also voted against legislation banning gender-transition care for minors, including puberty blockers and hormone therapy.

Mr. Talarico described God as “nonbinary” during one debate on the sports bill and said there were six sexes in another.

“Modern science obviously recognizes that there are many more than two biological sexes — in fact, there are six,” Mr. Talarico said in 2021, during a committee debate, before listing chromosomal variations associated with intersex people.

Now, as a Senate candidate, Mr. Talarico is attempting to revise some of those remarks. He now describes the statement that God is nonbinary as intentionally “provocative.” Although he voted against the treatment ban, he emphasizes that he supported an amendment to the bill to restrict surgeries for minors.

In September, in an interview on Fox News, Mr. Talarico said he opposed transgender athletes playing in girls’ sports if it endangered safety or fairness. His campaign said this view on athletic participation predated his run for federal office, but it did not provide examples of when he expressed this opinion before this year.

“There are not six sexes,” Mr. Talarico told Fox News. “There are two.”

On “The Daily,” he said it was Republican lawmakers, not him, who “were obsessed with talking about trans issues, were obsessed with talking about people’s private parts.”

“It’s not like I ran for the Legislature to talk about these things,” Mr. Talarico said.

Even as he found himself on the losing side in legislative battles, Mr. Talarico displayed a talent for sharp oratory and withering lines of questioning that drew attention.

“He will excoriate you like you’re Satan himself and then, three seconds later, act like he’s your best friend,” said Tom Oliverson, the chairman of the House Republican Caucus, who sponsored the 2023 ban on gender-transition care for minors.

“I like James on a personal level,” he added. “But there is a lot of performative theater that is James Talarico.”

The shift in Mr. Talarico’s public profile that would help make him a national progressive figure began in the summer of 2021.

Democrats in the Texas House, including Mr. Talarico, objected to new voting restrictions pushed by Republicans. They left the state to halt the proceedings and went to Washington seeking a national spotlight.

From the nation’s capital, at just 32 years old, Mr. Talarico emerged as a de facto spokesman for Texas Democrats. He appeared on national television and once sparred with Pete Hegseth live on Fox News, when Mr. Hegseth, now the defense secretary, was a host.

Upon returning to Austin, Mr. Talarico found himself targeted in a new way. In the process of redrawing the state’s voting maps, Republicans moved his district’s lines to make his re-election all but impossible.

To remain in the Texas House, Mr. Talarico opted to run for an open seat in the liberal enclave of Austin, where his parents lived.

The move set off a change in how he presented himself.

Mr. Talarico’s website no longer described him as “a proud Democrat who works with Republicans.” Instead, it cast him as “the most effective progressive at the Texas Capitol” who was “fighting back against Republican extremism.”

“I think the Republicans have created a monster,” Mr. Talarico wrote about himself on Facebook that fall, after acknowledging that being drawn out of his district had been “tough.”

Joe Moody, a longtime Democratic lawmaker and early mentor, said the experience of getting “burned” during redistricting shaped Mr. Talarico’s future political path. He won the 2022 election easily.

“His voice got a lot louder after that happened,” Mr. Moody said.

When lawmakers returned to Austin, Republicans put forward a slate of new hard-line conservative bills on everything from education to L.G.B.T.Q. rights. In response, Mr. Talarico spent the next two sessions as a vocal opponent of these measures, including bills restricting books in public-school libraries and further limiting abortion access.

Mr. Talarico’s spokesman, JT Ennis, argued that such opposition to Republican priorities was not inherently partisan.

“Calling out extreme legislation that a majority of Texans oppose,” Mr. Ennis said, “is bipartisan.”

Still, Mr. Talarico found issues on which to team up with Republicans. He joined Republican lawmakers to fight high prescription-drug prices and create a new state commission “to promote lasting marriage” and “two-parent households.” He worked on laws to combat opioid overdoses with Republican state senators, including Angela Paxton, Mr. Paxton’s wife.

“James has strong progressive values,” said Erin Zwiener, a Democratic state representative who was first elected the same year as Mr. Talarico, “and he’s eminently practical.”

In partisan rankings of lawmakers by Rice University based on their voting record, Mr. Talarico usually fell just left of the middle among Democrats. Despite being in a more liberal district, he passed more laws during his second two terms, The Times analysis found.

Among his colleagues, Mr. Talarico stood out as something of a grind. When fellow Texas lawmakers invited him out for drinks, he’d usually decline, colleagues recalled. “Did you ever go to school with someone who carries a briefcase?” said Dan Huberty, a former Republican state representative. “That’s him.”

Before entering politics, Mr. Talarico spent two years teaching sixth-grade at a San Antonio public school. Building on this experience, he later worked with rural Republicans to oppose using public funding for private school vouchers.

“He and I have some philosophical differences,” said Gary VanDeaver, a rural Republican lawmaker. “But that didn’t mean we couldn’t work together on some good public education policy.”

Mr. Talarico made his Christian faith central to his arguments against socially conservative bills. In 2022, he enrolled at Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary.

The following year, Mr. Talarico criticized a bill requiring the Ten Commandments in public schools as “un-American.” In 2024, he gave a sermon against Christian nationalism, and said it was “perverting my faith.” His remarks caught the attention of the podcaster Joe Rogan, who endorsed Mr. Trump that year.

Mr. Talarico appeared on Mr. Rogan’s podcast in July 2025. In a subsequent conversation with Vice President JD Vance roughly a year later, Mr. Rogan said Mr. Talarico had made “a really good point” and that requiring the Ten Commandments in public schools was “not the right way to do it.”

When a Ten Commandments bill came up again in 2025, Mr. Talarico asked its Republican sponsor why debate was scheduled on the mandatory day of rest in the commandments.

“You’d rather tell people to follow the Ten Commandments than follow it yourself?” he asked. A video of the exchange has collected 1.6 million likes on his TikTok account. The bill passed anyway.

item.title: His Election Could Decide Senate Control. He Could Make History, Too.
item.description:
It was a Friday night in an ornate New Hampshire opera house, and Representative Chris Pappas, the Democratic candidate for Senate here, had nearly finished his finely tuned stump speech.

He had slammed Washington corruption, promised to fight for affordable health care and lamented high prices, hewing to the message that Democrats across the country believe will win them back control of the Senate.

Mr. Pappas didn’t mention the man in plaid, standing amid the voters on the creaking wooden floor, who may nevertheless represent the most remarkable aspect of his candidacy: his husband.

Mr. Pappas, 46, is running a closer-than-expected campaign against former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican, a race that both parties view as critical. If he wins, he will be the first openly gay man to serve in the Senate — but this is not something he’s made central to his campaign.

“I’m not thinking much about history right now,” Mr. Pappas said in an interview. “I’m really thinking every day about the struggles of New Hampshire.”

His low-key approach to breaking a barrier mirrors that of some other Democratic Senate candidates this year, as a party burned by losses in cycles past backs away from identity politics. Former Representative Mary Peltola of Alaska talks little about the fact that she would be the first — or tied for the first — Native American female senator. In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed’s Muslim faith has become the target of political attacks. But on the trail, he talks more about how he would be the first Democratic doctor elected to the Senate in decades than the fact that he would be the first Muslim in the chamber.

Mr. Pappas’s understated approach to his potential pathbreaking reflects his generation as well as the way that his state, with its libertarian leanings, has become more accepting of gay rights over the course of his decades-long political career. Mr. Sununu has left the matter alone.

But it also comes at a fraught national moment, as some gay rights activists warn of the potential for backsliding. Just last week, Vice President JD Vance made fun of James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, by suggesting falsely that he was gay.

“We are seeing some incredibly cynical attacks on the L.G.B.T.Q. community today that have been mainstreamed in our politics, and people in the community are scared for where this country is headed,” Mr. Pappas said in an interview.

Still, he said, his constituents have been broadly accepting.

“Our state motto is ‘Live Free or Die,’ ” he said. “I think people, regardless of their politics, really just want their neighbors to be able to be themselves.”

If there is one thing New Hampshire voters know about Chris Pappas, it’s probably not the fact that he’s gay. It’s the chicken tenders.

He grew up in Manchester, where he was a fixture at the Puritan Backroom, the longstanding Pappas family restaurant where his grandfather is said to have invented the chicken tender. It has been a regular campaign stop for candidates for Congress and the White House for years. (Mr. Pappas is a co-owner of the business today.)

Mr. Pappas, who attended one of the state’s largest public high schools, wasn’t sure he would ever be embraced by his community as a gay man. There was no gay-straight alliance there, nor a single out student, as far as he knew.

“I’m living a reality today that I didn’t think was possible when I was growing up just a few decades ago,” he said.

But he came out at Harvard, and wove his identity into a political career that began when he came home and ran for state representative at the age of 22. “It’s not like I put a bullet point on my palm card, but I was very open about who I was,” Mr. Pappas said. Kathy Sullivan, the former chair of the New Hampshire Democratic Party, said Mr. Pappas’s sexual orientation has rarely become much of an issue in his campaigns.

“I can’t tell you there was a moment when I went, ‘Oh, Chris Pappas is a gay man,’” she said. “It’s just not a big deal.”

“People who knew, knew,” Mr. Pappas said. “And then I think as the battles kind of raged on issues around equality, I found my voice and was regularly speaking out on those issues.”

Pushing for gay rights became a key theme in his career.

In those years — the mid-aughts — New Hampshire was reckoning with gay marriage, which the highest court in Massachusetts, just over the border, had just deemed legal. Mr. Pappas delivered his first floor speech in 2004, when the state Legislature took up a bill to ban the recognition of those marriages.

“Everyone must see this bill for what it is,” Mr. Pappas said then. “It’s an anti-gay bill, plain and simple. No matter how it’s dressed up. No matter how it’s portrayed. No matter how it’s amended.”

That bill passed. By 2007, though, Gov. John Lynch had signed legislation legalizing civil unions — making New Hampshire the first state to do so without a court order or a pending lawsuit. In 2009, six years before it was legal nationwide, Mr. Lynch signed gay marriage into law in New Hampshire. By then, Mr. Pappas was treasurer of Hillsborough County. He lost re-election in 2010, before he was elected to the state’s Executive Council in 2012 and then to Congress in 2018.

In Washington, where he has served four terms in the House, he became co-chair of the Equality Caucus and has, over the years, sponsored or supported several gay rights measures, including one that would expand federal civil rights protections for gay and transgender Americans, and another that would protect benefits for gay, lesbian or transgender veterans discharged from the military because of their sexual orientation or their gender identity.

He is now running to replace Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the three-term Democrat who is not seeking re-election. His understated style mirrors hers.

In 2020, Mr. Pappas was running for re-election to Congress when his Republican opponent, Matt Mowers, used the debate stage to lob one of the biggest attacks of that campaign: Mr. Pappas, he said, had been dating an Amazon lobbyist while voting on bills that Amazon had lobbied on.

“That’s not true,” Mr. Pappas said, shaking his head.

Mr. Mowers did not mention the fact that the lobbyist in question, Vann Bentley, was a man, but Mr. Pappas and some gay rights organizations suggested the attack was rooted in homophobia.

Six years on, that exchange is a fixture of attack ads by Republicans’ main Senate super PAC against Mr. Pappas in this campaign. At least one ad shows images of Mr. Bentley, who is now Mr. Pappas’s husband; another never makes it clear that Mr. Pappas is in a same-sex relationship.

“My husband’s work has always been separate from mine,” Mr. Pappas said, accusing “dark money groups” of trying to “muddy the waters.”

(There is no evidence that Mr. Pappas lied about the existence of the relationship; the bills in question, which Amazon supported, were sweeping measures like government funding and defense measures, and Mr. Pappas’s votes lined up with much of his caucus’s.)

At times, Mr. Pappas has tried to neutralize personal attacks with wry humor. In September, the National Republican Senatorial Committee included a photo of Mr. Pappas and his cat, Dorothy, in a photo collage it posted on social media that also contained an image of Dr. El-Sayed dressed up as a character from “Blue’s Clues,” and Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate in Maine, drinking bubble tea.

“How does the left keep finding such normal men?” the post asked.

“I have a cat,” Mr. Pappas responded, “and John Sununu’s name is in the Epstein files.” (In a 2010 email, the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein suggested that an associate meet up with “john sununu, has good stories.” It is unclear whether that was a reference to Mr. Sununu or his father, John H. Sununu, the former New Hampshire governor. Mr. Sununu’s campaign said neither man ever communicated with Mr. Epstein or with the associate.)

Barney Frank of Massachusetts had been in the House of Representatives for six years when, in 1987, he became the first member of Congress to voluntarily come out, shortly after a closeted colleague died of AIDS.

It would be another quarter century before an openly gay candidate was elected to the Senate: Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin, in 2012. (Since then, Kyrsten Sinema, who is bisexual, and Laphonza Butler, who is gay, have joined and left the chamber.)

So, to gay rights advocates across the nation, the election of Mr. Pappas would represent a major milestone.

“It feels like something you’d want to sing from the rooftops,” said Mayor Matt Gerding of Somersworth, N.H., who said he is the state’s second out gay mayor. But he said he understood why Mr. Pappas’s campaign doesn’t.

“I think they know that, New Hampshire and many people in New Hampshire, aren’t looking for a candidate to necessarily check boxes and make history,” Mr. Gerding said. “They’re looking for a candidate that is honest, and putting their interests first.”

Mr. Pappas was joined this month on the campaign trail by Pete Buttigieg, who is perhaps the nation’s most prominent gay politician. (The two overlapped at Harvard for two years, although Mr. Buttigieg did not come out until later in life, when he was 33.)

But at a packed campaign office and again at the opera house, they assailed national Republicans while leaving it to young organizers who took the stage before or after them to spell out the history they could make.

“It’s because of Secretary Buttigieg and Congressman Pappas that I came out to my family and friends and discovered that the people around me truly loved me for who I was,” one organizer, Calvin Wood, said in Manchester.

In an interview, Mr. Buttigieg said it would be meaningful if Mr. Pappas breaks a barrier. But it wouldn’t be the point of his campaign.

“I think every campaign is about the voters much more than it’s about the candidate,” Mr. Buttigieg said. “And the most important thing about the candidate is: Are they prepared to stand up for what the voters most want?”

Michael Kruse contributed reporting, and Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Higher, Faster, Gnarlier: Have Roller Coasters Become Too Extreme?
item.description:
Compared with baseball and apple pie, the roller coaster is the renegade symbol of the carefree American summer.

It is a twisted beacon over the kaleidoscopic amusement-park landscape. It dares us to be daring. Steep drops, high speeds and improbably tight curves force screams from contorted faces and cause butterflies for those crowding to be next.

For the American leisure class, there is no entertainment quite like it. The roller coaster can be a rite of passage for kids and an obsession for adults.

Their continued popularity depends on a mind trick, a bit of dynamic tension — enticing us to strap into something that feels dangerous, maybe unwise, but is actually safe.

“The goal is to flirt with danger without actually experiencing it,” said Brian Avery, a University of Florida lecturer who specializes in amusement-park safety. “But occasionally, people are exposed to it, and they’re either dying or are being significantly injured as a result of it.”

This month, a new round of reckoning has arrived.

On Oct. 12, a man was thrown from his seat, mid-ride, and died on the Goliath coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia. That prompted Six Flags, the chain of amusement parks, to shut down at least nine other coasters across the country for closer inspection.

Only weeks earlier, in late September, Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, Calif., permanently closed one of its popular coasters, X2, after years of complaints about its safety. It faced a lawsuit from three riders regarding catastrophic brain injuries, and recently settled a wrongful-death suit involving a 22-year-old man who died a day after riding the coaster in 2022.

Concern over roller-coaster safety is not a new issue. It rises and falls with every technological twist of gut-bending, mind-blowing adaptations. Each generation of coaster becomes higher, faster, steeper, bendier and gnarlier. And maybe more worrisome.

Have roller coasters, finally, gone too far? Have we reached the point where they can’t get more thrilling, or death-defying, because of limits in technology, safety or human physiology?

Probably not, experts said. Tomorrow’s coasters will certainly have the capability of flinging around people in more extreme ways.

But should they?

“I don’t know that we’ve explored the limits of, Is that good for a person?” Mr. Avery said.

The only sure thing is that more coasters are on the way.

“In our industry, the coaster is still king,” said Dennis Speigel, a global theme-park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions.

“When you want attendance to pop at your park or in your company, you don’t put in a carousel, you don’t put in a scrambler, you put in a roller coaster, and you name it ‘The Demon’ or ‘The Bat’ or ‘The Beast’ or whatever,” he said. “And people come out in droves to ride it.”

The history of fatal coaster rides includes mechanical failures, people falling out, heart attacks and other medical ailments.

The deadliest incident in the United States occurred in 1930, on a coaster in Omaha called “The Big Dipper.” A loose bolt caused a crash that killed four people and injured 17.

In 1972, in England, a chain pulling a coaster uphill snapped, sending cars backward and killing five people.

The idea of attaching small, wheeled cars to rails for thrills, not just transport, goes back about 200 years. But it was in the United States in the late 1800s that so-called gravity rides truly took shape.

Slews of patents were filed — to pull cars uphill, to link multiple cars together, to bring cars to a stop. By 1888, an inventor named LaMarcus Adna Thompson had built dozens of coasters in the United States and Europe, including the Switchback Railway in Coney Island in New York.

By 1895, the Flip Flap at Sea Lion Park in Coney Island took riders for a loop, literally, after its safety was tested by sand bags and monkeys. Its tight circle-shaped loop — not the larger teardrop of modern times — created G-forces beyond the 4 or 5 Gs that some coasters exert today. It left untold riders limping away with whiplash and spine injuries before it closed in 1902.

But Coney Island’s long history of coasters was just getting rolling, and not always safely. In 1910, three people died on the Rough Riders coaster when it took a curve too fast, flipped over and ejected 17 riders.

The ride lost its license, just temporarily. Five summers later, five people flew out. “Passengers were shot out of their seats and hurled against the double railing of one-inch iron piping which bordered the track for about 40 feet above the entrance,” The New York Times reported. “The railing broke under the impact, and the passengers were flung headlong down to the crowded pavement.” A passing priest delivered last rites.

The two survivors were a mother and son; she had somehow clung to a railing with one arm, dangling above the crowd, while holding her 4-year-old child, the Times account said.

Soon came the invention of securing wheels under the rails, instead of between them like a train car. That led to steeper, more contorted coasters.

By the 1920s, the country had 1,500 roller coasters, none more famous than the Cyclone in Coney Island. The clattering loop, with an 85-foot plunge and speeds of up to 60 miles per hour, is still there, a historical landmark.

Coaster popularity faded with the Depression and World War II. But Disneyland opened in 1955, and its Matterhorn helped spark a new era: relatively smooth rides on tubular steel.

In 1975, the Corkscrew at Knott’s Berry Farm in California turned riders upside down and held them in place with over-the-shoulder harnesses. A year later, the Revolution at Magic Mountain featured a vertical loop, which was quickly imitated.

Before long, there were propulsion systems that shot cars as if from a cannon. There were coasters where riders’ feet dangled free, and others that stood riders up or laid them flat to give the sensation of flying. There were coasters that went backward. There were coasters with up to 10 loops.

The first 100 m.p.h. coaster — the 415-foot-tall “Superman: Escape From Krypton” ride at Magic Mountain — opened in 1997.

Then came X, renamed X2 after a redesign in 2008.

“X is just the latest ploy in a constant game of technological one-upmanship played by amusement parks every summer to attract the masochistic masses,” Forbes wrote in 2001 before the ride opened.

Aside from the loops and drops, the article said, “the cars spin 360 degrees, sending passengers head over heels like Mary Lou Retton on a tumbling routine strapped to the Cyclone.”

The revolution continues. Last December, Falcons Flight opened in Saudi Arabia. It set records for the fastest (155 m.p.h.), tallest (535 feet) and longest coaster (nearly 14,000 feet, or about 2.6 miles).

“If you can think it, it gets created,” said Mr. Avery, the University of Florida lecturer. “And as long as an engineer establishes tolerances that the average person can continue to be safe while experiencing it, I don’t know where it ends.”

Last Friday at Magic Mountain — “The Thrill Capital of the World,” where the daily pass at the window costs $110 for adults — there were the familiar sights and sounds of the roller coasters, the clacking and whooshing of cars, riders screaming and laughing.

Goliath, one of the coasters that Six Flags had closed after the Georgia incident — the two rides share a name but have different designs and manufacturers — was open again.

The gate to X2 was locked and the sign was gone. Under construction elsewhere in the park, though, was Thrill Glider, a “suspended glider train” with five inversions. It is expected to open next year.

Darien Lewis and his fiancée, Melissa Bethel, both 36, are season-pass holders. He loves the coasters. She goes along but is scared of heights.

They knew about X2’s closing — “The scariest ride I’ve ever been on,” he said — but had not heard that someone fell out and died on a coaster in Georgia.

“Oh my god,” Ms. Bethel said.

“That’s the only thing I fear,” Mr. Lewis said.

“That is terrifying,” she said, adding, “He’ll still go.”

“I’ll still go,” he said. “I’ll just be thinking of that now.”

“But rides are never going to be perfect,” she said. “You just never know. Anything could happen.”

The International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions reports that about one injury occurs for every million coaster rides in North America. A 2004 study found that an average of four people had died on coasters each year over the previous decade.

Mr. Speigel, the consultant, noted that the recent death in Georgia was the coaster’s first known fatal incident since a man died of a heart attack on the ride shortly after it opened in 2006.

“If they’re not safe, the manufacturers are out of business,” Mr. Speigel said.

But Mr. Avery, whose father was safety director at Busch Gardens in Florida, advocates changes. Among them: better and more transparent reporting of injuries and safety problems; federal oversight instead of a hodgepodge of state and local jurisdictions and self-regulation among the biggest parks; and better guidance for people trying to decide if the ride is really a good idea.

In interviews last week with coaster riders at the Cedar Point theme park in Ohio and at Magic Mountain in California, most were aware of the recent fatality but undeterred about climbing aboard.

“Hearing about that death doesn’t make me scared to die when I get on a roller coaster,” said Jenna Kulhawuk, 32, a videographer visiting Cedar Point. “I’ve never been like that — afraid of things that won’t happen.”

Among the riders of Goliath at Magic Mountain on Friday was Alexa Montoya, 20, visiting with several friends. She knew about the incident in Georgia, and before she left home her mother had told her to take extra care to strap in.

Ms. Montoya and her friends were all laughs and smiles as they got off the ride.

“I definitely got an adrenaline high,” Ms. Montoya said.

“Dude, I, like, almost passed out,” her friend said.

“Yeah, not gonna lie,” Ms. Montoya said. “I did almost pass out, but I was remembering, like, ‘Breathe, breathe.’”

They were tickled by the thrill more than they were worried about the danger.

“It seems simple in nature,” Mr. Avery said. “You walk up the platform, you get on the train, and you’re dispatched. And you’re delivered back to that platform in the same shape in which you left. That’s the goal.”

Esmé E. Deprez contributed reporting from Valencia, Calif., and Dan McGraw from Sandusky, Ohio.

Recent headlines about roller coasters have sparked concerns — not for the first time — over safety. For the thrill-seekers: are today's rides pushing the envelope too far or are you still first in line, no matter how wild and extreme they get?

item.title: Reliably Red Iowa in Play as Economic Woes Mount
item.description:
The diesel fuel that powers the tractors and combines on Kelly Nieuwenhuis’s 3,000-acre Iowa farm costs almost double what it did earlier this year because of the war in Iran. Fertilizer prices are also rising, as Russia’s war in Ukraine drags on. And sales of the corn and soybeans that he grows have been depressed amid trade fights with China, Canada and Mexico.

Mr. Nieuwenhuis, a registered Republican, voted for Donald J. Trump in 2016 and 2020, but not in 2024. He is frustrated with Mr. Trump’s policies as president, and plans to split his ticket in the midterm elections. He will support Rob Sand, the Democratic candidate for governor, but is backing Ashley Hinson, the Republican running for Senate.

“It’s the economy, stupid,” said Mr. Nieuwenhuis, echoing a political slogan that has doomed Republicans in the past.

He recalled spending $16,000 to fill up the fuel tanks on his farm in Primghar, Iowa, this fall. “Every election it comes down to the economy, and this policy is not working,” he said. “The Iran war, all the energy costs, the inflation — everything has gone up in price drastically.”

The country’s economic crosscurrents are cascading across Iowa. High gas prices, elevated interest rates and Mr. Trump’s unpredictable economic policies, including tariffs, have been battering rural America over the last year. Iowa’s economy contracted in 2025 and notched the weakest annual growth rate in the country, according to the federal Bureau of Economic Analysis.

Polls suggest that the state that helped propel Mr. Trump’s political rise could flip in favor of Democrats when voters cast their ballots next month.

The stakes are so high that Mr. Trump will head to Sioux City, Iowa, on Thursday to try and convince a once-stalwart Republican base to keep his party in control of Congress. He is expected to promote the $8 billion in economic aid to farmers hurt by high diesel prices that he announced on Monday night. It was the second time in two years that the president authorized billions of dollars in bailout money for farmers harmed by his administration’s policies.

The payouts are papering over a painful economic problem for Iowa’s farmers, who were hurt by international backlash to Mr. Trump’s tariffs in his first term and never fully recovered. Farmland values in the state have been tepid in recent years, and farm bankruptcies were up by 220 percent last year.

The economic doldrums in the state have spread, with big companies such as John Deere, Wells Fargo and Whirlpool announcing job cuts in Iowa in recent months.

Mr. Trump’s argument to let Republicans keep political power in Washington and Iowa could be a tough sell.

The Iowa Farmers Union, one of the state’s oldest farm organizations, backed the entire Democratic congressional slate this cycle, breaking a decades-long streak of abstaining from federal endorsements.

Matt Russell, a farmer and the group’s executive director, said that its members had been frustrated with Mr. Trump and the state’s Republican congressional delegation long before the war. He cited cuts to federal programs benefiting farmers, cancellations of promised grants and the expiration of Affordable Care Act health insurance subsidies.

The Iran war and trade tensions have only added to the strain farmers were feeling, he said, as rising costs have eaten into their slim margins.

“Republican leadership at the federal level has not been standing up to this administration and has not been actually delivering the investments that we were counting on,” Mr. Russell said.

Some top Republicans, including Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa, have pleaded with the Trump administration to do more to help the state’s economy. Last year, Mr. Grassley called on Mr. Trump to exempt potash, an ingredient in fertilizer, from the tariffs the president imposed on Canada. He recently called on the White House to temporarily ban diesel fuel exports, saying it would “help family farmers.”

Peter Orazem, an economist at Iowa State University, said that economic output in Iowa had been far slower than most other states over the previous five years, recording an average annual growth rate of just 1 percent since 2021.

The state is not just vulnerable to dramatic changes in the agricultural sector. Tariffs have increased manufacturing production costs in the state, and Mr. Trump’s immigration policies have made labor costs more expensive. The president’s aversion to wind and solar has also weighed on Iowa’s renewable energy sector.

“Iowa is basically lagging the rest of the U.S. pretty much across the board,” Mr. Orazem said. “I believe that there are few states that have been more disadvantaged by Trump policies than Iowa.”

The agricultural concerns in Iowa also go beyond corn and soybeans.

The Iowa Cattlemen’s Association, which represents beef producers, has also expressed frustration about some of Mr. Trump’s trade policies. In August, the group criticized his decision to cut tariffs on 300,000 metric tons of ground beef, saying the move to sell meat below market rate would hurt struggling ranchers.

Economists said the imports would not significantly affect consumer prices. But they caused cattle futures to drop by hundreds of dollars, influencing the prices cattle ranchers could negotiate for at market. Numerous Midwestern Republican lawmakers, including Ms. Hinson, pushed back against the imports.

The executive director of the Iowa Cattlemen’s Association, Bryan Whaley, said that some of the Trump administration’s policies, and Mr. Trump’s comments, had driven market volatility, which he called the main challenge facing cattle ranchers in Iowa. But he said that ups and downs were part of working with any president.

“As in every administration, you’re always going to have things that you appreciate and some things that are done that you may not necessarily agree with,” Mr. Whaley, a rancher, said when asked about Mr. Trump’s performance.

Mr. Whaley added that the state’s congressional delegation had been “extremely receptive” to the group’s concerns.

The political arm of the Iowa Farm Bureau, the state’s largest grass roots farm organization, endorsed Ms. Hinson and all four Republican House nominees. But the group’s political action committee, which has historically supported Republicans at the top of the ticket, declined to endorse in the governor’s race. The group did not respond to a request for comment on the decision. The Democratic nominee, Mr. Sand, has appealed to Republicans and swing voters with a centrist message.

The backlash to Mr. Trump’s policies has Democrats feeling emboldened.

Josh Turek, the Democratic nominee for Senate, has slammed Republicans over high diesel prices and Mr. Trump’s tariffs on potash, which is largely imported from Canada. Last week, Mr. Turek visited the farm of a three-time Trump voter, Marcus Tomlonovic, to drive the point home.

Mr. Tomlonovic, a 30-year-old corn and soybean farmer in Colfax, Iowa, said he was planning to vote for Mr. Turek and other Democrats because he was frustrated that Mr. Trump had entered a foreign war after promising to stay out of them.

“I feel like we’ve been betrayed,” Mr. Tomlonovic said in a phone interview, adding that diesel had cost him an additional $1,000 each week. “How much more are we going to take before small farmers can’t hang on?”

Derek Eadon, a Democratic strategist from West Des Moines, said he was “cautiously optimistic” that Mr. Trump’s unpopularity would help Democrats perform well in November.

“The Iowa Republican Party has been in lock step with Trump the entire way since he’s been in office,” Mr. Eadon said. “And I don’t think there’s any getting away from that at the very end with a tweet or a vote here or there.”

In a state Republicans have dominated since 2016, when Mr. Trump flipped it after Barack Obama twice won it, major races have become unexpectedly competitive. Mr. Sand has led the Republican nominee, Zach Lahn, in every major nonpartisan poll this year.

Ms. Hinson, the Republican nominee for Senate, is neck-and-neck with Mr. Turek, a state representative. And Republican candidates in three of the state’s four congressional districts have struggled to establish clear leads over Democratic opponents.

“We do need to find ways to provide relief to our farmers who are at the fields every single day in the middle of harvest,” Ms. Hinson told reporters at an event this week in Des Moines, where she discussed pausing the diesel gas tax. “I think long term we need to be focusing on more refining capacity here in the United States.”

This week, the main super PAC supporting House Republicans canceled its ad reservations in the swing district held by Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks, a Republican, signaling that the party no longer saw a path for the second-term lawmaker. Senate Republicans’ top super PAC has spent more than $40 million on advertising in Iowa to support Ms. Hinson, according to the media tracking firm AdImpact, a staggering sum in a state that Mr. Trump won by 13 points in 2024.

The political environment is “brutal” for Republicans in Iowa, said Alex Conant, a Republican consultant who has worked on Senate and presidential campaigns in the state.

“If the economy is the number one issue everywhere,” Mr. Conant said, “it’s the only issue in Iowa.”

Some Republican farmers are still planning to stick with their party.

Jolene Riessen, who grows corn and soybeans on her family farm in Ida Grove, is spending $6,000 every week to 10 days to fill fuel tanks with diesel. She has had to sell a dry spreader truck and a tractor to save money to offset the higher costs.

But she does not blame Mr. Trump for invading Iran, and thinks that oil companies are using that as an excuse to hike prices on consumers. She will continue to back Republican candidates even though inflation is making her life harder.

“I haven’t really seen the Democrats do me a lot of favors,” Ms. Riessen said. “I mean, I just go back to the Biden administration. What do they do for the farmer?”

item.title: Covert Russian Group Injects Baseless Claim Into the Texas Senate Race
item.description:
Even as President Trump pursued a thawing of relations with the Kremlin this week, a covert Russian influence operation targeted the Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate in Texas, James Talarico, by spreading a fabricated claim of misconduct.

Several groups of researchers who track Russian disinformation operations attributed the claim to Storm-1516, a covert group that in 2024 peddled a similarly unfounded accusation against Gov. Tim Walz of Minnesota, who was the Democratic vice-presidential nominee.

The attack followed a flurry of Russian posts on social media in recent weeks and provided the latest indication that Moscow is once again targeting an American election with online influence operations. In recent weeks, Russia has ramped up those efforts, according to a U.S. official familiar with classified intelligence assessments on the matter.

Most of the Russian content so far, spread by bot networks around the world, has targeted Democratic candidates, especially in closely contested Senate races that could determine control of Congress in Mr. Trump’s remaining two years in office. Still, the intelligence assessments do not specify that Russia is explicitly seeking to harm one political party more than the other, the official said.

“I characterize it to people as kind of same old, same old,” Representative Jim Himes of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, said on Wednesday, referring broadly to Russian efforts so far this campaign. The Russians are “throwing everything out there to generate a sense of chaos and anarchy” in the voting process, he added.

Mr. Himes said Russia was focused “in a bipartisan way” on trying to harm American politicians who had been supportive of Ukraine.

The video targeting Mr. Talarico appeared as Mr. Trump’s special envoy, Steve Witkoff, visited Moscow as part the administration’s efforts to press for an end to the war in Ukraine and more broadly tensions between the United States and Russia.

In remarks broadcast on state television in Russia, Mr. Witkoff praised President Vladimir V. Putin on Wednesday as a humanitarian for agreeing to release an imprisoned American who was living in Ukraine when Russian forces invaded in 2022.

The claim about Mr. Talarico appeared on Tuesday morning in a video posted on X on an account that had been created last month. Mr. Talarico is locked in a heated Senate race against Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas.

A week ago, Republican opponents spread a baseless claim that Mr. Talarico had traveled to Ohio for medical treatment.

A spokesman for the Talarico campaign, JT Ennis, said on Wednesday, “The most powerful people in the world know they can’t beat James Talarico with the truth, so they’re slandering him with A.I. deepfakes, foreign bots and conspiracy theories to protect their broken, corrupt political system.”

The initial post on Tuesday, followed by others on the same account, received little attention until 12 hours later, when three verified accounts on X with large followings reposted it.

Storm-1516 previously used those accounts to spread disinformation, according to analyses by Alethea, a threat intelligence company, and Clemson University’s Media Forensics Hub. Storm-1516 operates closely with a Russian organization with ties to the Kremlin, the Foundation to Battle Injustice.

Another threat analysis company, Graphika, said the video — and a second that appeared later — appeared to have been generated by artificial intelligence tools.

According to Alethea, the video was viewed more than 850,000 in the first 24 hours.

Darren L. Linvill, a founder of the Media Forensics Hub who has tracked Storm-1516 closely, said the video simply recycled a playbook from the 2024 election, but he suggested that Russia was intensifying its influence efforts before Nov. 3.

“Now that they’ve started,” he said, “there will be other opportunities.”

item.title: Manosphere Influencer Clavicular Pleads Not Guilty to Rape Charge
item.description:
Clavicular, the social media influencer who exhorts young men to improve their appearance through “looksmaxxing,” pleaded not guilty to a rape charge on Thursday in a Massachusetts court.

The 20-year-old, whose real name is Braden Peters, appeared in person for the brief arraignment in Orleans, Mass., on Cape Cod.

In September, Mr. Peters was charged with assaulting a 17-year-old girl at a home owned by his family on the Cape. According to a police report, he served the girl alcohol at the house while livestreaming in May 2025, and had sex with her several times after the broadcast ended. The police later concluded, based on her likely level of intoxication, that she lacked the capacity to consent.

At the arraignment in Orleans District Court on Thursday, a judge set bail at $10,000. Prosecutors agreed to the bail amount after Mr. Peters, who wore a dark suit and tie with glasses and arrived at the courthouse with a dog that barked at reporters, flew from California for the appearance. The next court date is set for Nov. 24.

Mr. Peters posted bail immediately after the hearing. As part of his bail conditions, he agreed to surrender his passport, stay away from the plaintiff, and refrain from posting about her online.

He spoke only once during the arraignment, responding “Yes, your honor,” when Judge John Julian asked him if he understood that he could be held without bail if he commits a new offense. He left the courthouse without speaking to reporters.

Mr. Peters faces two felony charges — one count of rape and one count of drugging someone to facilitate sexual intercourse — and a misdemeanor charge of providing alcohol to someone under 21. If convicted of all charges, he could face penalties as severe as life in prison.

The plaintiff, who is now 18, also filed a civil lawsuit in Miami in April that made similar claims against Mr. Peters.

The criminal charges on Cape Cod were filed on Sept. 8. Soon afterward, Mr. Peters appeared to suggest in a post on X that his accuser had lied in hopes of winning a financial settlement: “Happens to all successful young men, people try to come for your money,” he wrote in the post. “Greed is evil.”

In her civil lawsuit, the plaintiff, who is also an influencer, said she had accepted Mr. Peters’s offer of an Uber ride to his family home on Cape Cod on May 23, 2025, because she thought it could bring more attention to her own social media presence. Mr. Peters’s mother and grandmother were at the house during the attack, the lawsuit states.

The plaintiff reported that Mr. Peters instructed her to lie and say that the alcohol he gave her was water while appearing on the livestream. She has also accused Mr. Peters of injecting her face with Aqualyx, a fat-dissolving substance, without her consent.

His lawyers have asked a judge in Miami to delay the civil court proceedings while the criminal case plays out in Massachusetts, so as to protect his right against possible self-incrimination.

In early October, the woman’s Florida lawyers filed an updated civil suit that dropped the sexual assault allegation, although it still asserted Mr. Peters gave her multiple drinks and had sex with her while she was intoxicated. The suit seeks damages for battery, fraud and intentional infliction of emotional distress, among other alleged offenses.

The Florida lawyers, in a statement, said the sex assault allegation was dropped because the woman did not “want her civil case to interfere” with the criminal proceedings in Massachusetts.

In his livestreams, which are routinely watched by thousands of viewers, Mr. Peters judges other people’s looks and discusses his own use of steroids, testosterone and other substances to enhance his appearance, or “ascend.”

Legal problems have ensnared Mr. Peters, whose lessons in looksmaxxing have won him a large and loyal following among young men striving to improve their attractiveness. He has been involved in several other criminal cases this year.

In February, he was arrested in Scottsdale, Ariz., and charged with having fake identification, an Adderall pill and an oral steroid. The charges were later dropped. The next month, he was arrested in Florida, accused of arranging a brawl between two women. Prosecutors dropped those charges, too.

Then in May, a Miami judge sentenced him to six months of probation for a misdemeanor weapons charge after he shot at a dead alligator during a livestream. Mr. Peters pleaded no contest.

item.title: Powerful Virginia Lawmaker Indicted Over Marijuana Business
item.description:
A powerful Democrat in the Virginia state legislature was charged on Thursday with running a criminal drug conspiracy through a marijuana dispensary business.

The legislator, L. Louise Lucas of Portsmouth, is an outspoken critic of the Trump administration who has long been a leading proponent of legal marijuana. She is also accused of conspiring to distribute marijuana, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The charges stemmed from an investigation that began during the Biden administration.

The evidence in the indictment against her lists business transactions of her marijuana dispensary, and a social media post she made in 2022 in which she wrote: “I’m a 78 year grandma who legalized pot and now has her own cannibis (sic) store. And I’m the last thing standing between the GOP and total control of Virginia.”

Ms. Lucas, the first Black woman to hold the post of Senate president pro tempore in Virginia, spearheaded an effort to redraw the state’s congressional district map heavily in favor of Democrats. That effort was eventually thrown out by the courts.

In May, F.B.I. agents searched Ms. Lucas’s business offices. A lawmaker for more than 30 years, she owns a network of group homes for older adults and a marijuana dispensary.

Ms. Lucas has denounced the investigation as an attempt to use federal law enforcement power to “intimidate and silence the voices who stood up to them.”

In February, after Republicans complained that the proposed Virginia political map was unfair to their voters, Ms. Lucas, who has been unafraid to throw punches, was characteristically blunt on social media.

“You all started it,” she replied to Senator Ted Cruz, Republican of Texas. “We,” she said, using an expletive, “finished it.”

She has become known for her trolling of Republicans, often skewering the former governor Glenn Youngkin, and helping block his efforts to use state incentives to draw a sports arena to Alexandria.

But she has also singled out the current governor, Abigail Spanberger, a fellow Democrat, over the issue of tax breaks for data centers, nicknaming her “Data Center Diva.”
