item.title: Ohio’s Republican Governor Calls on Ramaswamy to Take Down Attack Ad
item.description:
Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican, called Thursday on Vivek Ramaswamy, his party’s nominee to succeed him, to take down a widely criticized attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton.

It was a rare public rebuke of the campaign, which rejected his criticism and said it would keep running the ad, and put the governor at odds with Vice President JD Vance, another Ohio Republican, who told members of his party on Wednesday to “stop whining” about it.

“The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling,” Mr. DeWine told reporters on Thursday, and spoke about his work with rape and sexual assault survivors as a former prosecutor. He added, “It’s wrong to run this ad.”

The spot from Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign began circulating on social media this week and airing Thursday on television. In it, Donna Arthur, Dr. Acton’s birth mother, calls her daughter a “liar” and says that she fabricated stories about her difficult childhood.

Mr. DeWine said that in his experience working with Dr. Acton in state government, where she led the Ohio health department’s response to the Covid-19 pandemic, “she certainly told the truth.”

A grand jury in 1978 indicted Ms. Arthur’s husband — Dr. Acton’s stepfather — on charges of raping Dr. Acton, who was then a child, according to documents provided by the Acton campaign. The mother and daughter both say they have not spoken since that year, when Ms. Arthur lost custody of her daughter.

The stepfather, Cledith Arthur, pleaded not guilty, and then fled the state before trial, according to the court records. He died in Pennsylvania in 2004.

In his comments, Mr. DeWine declined to rescind his support of Mr. Ramaswamy and the rest of the Republican ticket, saying, “I did my endorsement a few months ago.” But he noted that campaign ads have reached “a new low” this year.

He said that family members should be “off limits,” and also chided the Acton campaign for issuing a news release that drew attention to the work that Mr. Ramaswamy’s mother, a doctor, had done as part of one of his business ventures. “But,” Mr. DeWine added in reference to the Ramaswamy ad, “this is on T.V., with $4 million behind it.”

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign dismissed Mr. DeWine’s call to stop running the ad in a response that focused on the Acton campaign’s news release, calling criticism of the attack ad a double standard. “Voters shouldn’t buy it,” said Connie Luck, a spokeswoman for the Ramaswamy campaign.

A series of Democrats and Republicans in Ohio have condemned the Ramaswamy ad this week. Several national Republican figures also stepped in to criticize it, including the former governors Chris Christie of New Jersey and Nikki Haley of South Carolina, who competed against Mr. Ramaswamy in the 2024 Republican presidential primary.

Dr. Acton’s brother, Philip Stearns, condemned the ad and said his sister had been the victim of their stepfather’s physical and sexual abuse for years. The candidate’s daughter, Madison Beech, also criticized the Ramaswamy campaign “for politicizing a family’s trauma in a desperate attempt to win an election” in a statement to The New York Times.

Former Representative Jim Renacci, an Ohio Republican, suggested on Thursday that Mr. Ramaswamy had hurt his prospects of winning the governor’s race by airing the ad. He also said that “sympathy can become a powerful political force” when “voters believe someone has been treated unfairly.”

“Elections aren’t won simply by convincing voters that your opponent is worse,” Mr. Renacci wrote on social media. “They’re won by convincing voters that you’re better.”

Mr. Ramaswamy’s campaign said Wednesday that it planned to spend $4 million airing the ad in Ohio.

item.title: Is Citizens United to Blame for Everything?
item.description:
Elon Musk is pouring astounding sums into supporting Republican candidates in the midterm elections. How can it be that the richest man in the world can lawfully deploy hundreds of millions of dollars to try to install his favored politicians?

The glib answer is that everything changed in 2010, when the Supreme Court ruled in the Citizens United case that corporations and unions have a First Amendment right to spend unlimited amounts in candidate elections.

But there are many misconceptions about Citizens United. A cleareyed look at the decision undermines the conventional view that it single-handedly opened the floodgates of dark money in American politics.

It did not, for instance, establish the principle that corporations have First Amendment rights.

As Justice John Paul Stevens acknowledged in his dissent, the court had long recognized that “corporations are covered by the First Amendment.” Justice Anthony Kennedy, writing for the majority, listed more than 20 precedents to that effect.

Nor is Citizens United responsible for the rise in dark money in elections. Indeed, the court upheld the disclosure requirements in the case by an 8-to-1 vote even as it voted 5 to 4 to strike down limits on corporate spending.

Citizens United was also but a chapter in a long saga. The decision that allowed individuals to spend without limit, Buckley v. Valeo, was decided half a century ago, in 1976.

Still, a new study in The Yale Law Journal Forum demonstrates that Citizens United marked a turning point — as a galvanizing symbol that seems to have affected judicial behavior in ways untethered to its actual holding.

“A lot of the complaints people have about the role of money in politics can’t neatly be traced to Citizens United itself,” said Duncan Hosie, the director of the Stanford Constitutional Law Center and the author of the study. But, he added, the decision was a potent shorthand for the Supreme Court’s campaign finance jurisprudence and the increasing influence of money on the political system, one that amped up partisan polarization among lower court judges.

The study examined about 800 First Amendment challenges to campaign finance regulations in the two decades after Chief Justice John Roberts joined the Supreme Court in 2005.

The rate at which Republican appointees upheld such regulations remained constant, at around 40 percent. But Democratic appointees’ behavior changed after Citizens United. The rate at which they upheld campaign finance regulations increased to 73 percent from 64 percent.

In this area and many others, ideology matters more as you move up the judicial ladder. There was a 15-percentage-point gap between Republican and Democratic appointees at the trial court level. It grew to 33 points in the appeals courts and to 81 points in the Supreme Court.

There was another kind of gap, too, one between appointees of different presidents. Fifty-two percentage points separated President Trump’s appointees, who upheld just 27 percent of regulations, and those of President Bill Clinton, who upheld 79 percent of them.

Before Citizens United, the politics of regulating the role of money in politics was more complicated. The formal name of the challenged law, after all, was the Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002. It was more commonly called the McCain-Feingold Act, cosponsored by Senator John McCain, Republican of Arizona, and Senator Russ Feingold, Democrat of Wisconsin.

People forget the details of the dispute. It involved a polemical documentary called “Hillary: The Movie,” a relentlessly negative look at Hillary Clinton’s career and character as she sought the Democratic nomination in 2008.

The documentary was made by a conservative advocacy group called Citizens United, which lost a lawsuit against the Federal Election Commission seeking permission to distribute it on a video-on-demand service. The McCain-Feingold law banned “electioneering communications” paid for by corporations within 30 days of a primary or 60 days of a general election.

The case divided some usual allies. Most liberal groups supported the law, while the American Civil Liberties Union backed Citizens United. That position was not popular with many A.C.L.U. members.

The group explained its stance in a 2012 statement.

“Our system of free expression,” the statement said, “is built on the premise that the people get to decide what speech they want to hear; it is not the role of the government to make that decision for them.”

A brief supporting Citizens United by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press said the McCain-Feingold law, which exempted news reports, commentaries and editorials, nonetheless posed unacceptable dangers.

“By criminalizing the distribution of a long-form documentary film as if it were nothing more than a very long advertisement,” the brief said, a lower court’s ruling “created uncertainty about where the line between traditional news commentary and felonious advocacy lies.”

The court had plenty of offramps. It could have focused, as the Reporters Committee suggested, on the differences between TV ads and documentaries. It could have distinguished between messages that you have to seek out and ones that arrive uninvited. It could have drawn a line between small advocacy groups and major public corporations.

The court instead went big, unleashing corporate and labor spending. That said, rich people like Musk were already free to spend unlimited sums under Buckley v. Valeo, which struck down limits on political spending by individuals in a 1971 law that was substantially amended in 1974 in the wake of Watergate.

A 2010 federal appeals court decision issued after Citizens United and said to flow from it made it easier for people like Musk to spend money through super PACs. But Citizens United by itself, Hosie said, “is not the root cause of his ability to use his fortune to influence political outcomes.”

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

Mailbag

In the Oct. 8 issue of The Docket, you mentioned that the judge in the James Comey seashell case decided not to accept friend-of-the-court briefs. Could you expand on what a friend-of-the-court brief is? — Phillip Visha, Columbus, Ga.

Lawyers call them “amicus curiae briefs,” and they are intended to help judges navigate difficult legal and factual issues. There was a time when they were isolated and disinterested efforts, typically from law professors. No more. People who claim to be friends of the court are now, almost without exception, actually friends of one party or the other.

Still, particularly in federal appeals courts and state Supreme Courts, such briefs can provide additional perspectives overlooked by the parties. In the U.S. Supreme Court, where the parties’ briefs are almost universally comprehensive and excellent, the additional briefs are generally pointless flag-waving exercises.

“The vast majority of amicus curiae briefs are filed by allies of litigants and duplicate the arguments made in the litigants’ briefs, in effect merely extending the length of the litigant’s brief,” Judge Richard A. Posner, then of the federal appeals court in Chicago, wrote in 1997. “Such amicus briefs should not be allowed. They are an abuse.”

Justices seem to have no objection to such briefs. But they are easy to ignore.

“Normally I didn’t even read amicus briefs,” Justice John Paul Stevens told me in 2011, a year after he retired.

“That was one of the tasks I assigned to my law clerks,” he said. “Their job was, if they thought an amicus brief really should be read, they’d pull them out for me and then I’d look at them.”

Justice Antonin Scalia, who died in 2016, said something similar in 2011 at Chicago-Kent College of Law, but more pungently.

“My law clerks read all amicus briefs,” he said. “If there’s one that has a hidden truffle in there somewhere, they call it to my attention.”

I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes.com.

Closing Argument

The Supreme Court announced on Monday that it could not hear a copyright case because four justices had recused themselves. A federal law and one of the court’s internal rules require a six-justice quorum to conduct any business.

Another federal law in essence directs a quorum-less court to affirm the judgment of the court below without issuing an opinion or setting a precedent.

The court’s order did not say why Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and Ketanji Brown Jackson had recused themselves, but it was almost certainly because they had published books with imprints of Penguin Random House, which shares a parent company, Bertelsmann, with one of the parties in the copyright case.

None of the four justices responded to my request for an explanation of why they had recused themselves.

The question in the case was whether a songwriter seeking to reclaim his rights to a song could do so not only in the United States but also around the world. In turning down a petition from BMG Rights Management and other publishers, the Supreme Court let stand a Fifth Circuit ruling in favor of the songwriter.

The court’s ethics rules allow the justices only a few ways to make money off the bench. They can teach, though there is an annual cap of roughly $35,000. And they can write books. Seven of the nine justices have done so or have a project underway, and they collectively made more than $13 million, according to a tally by Fix the Court, an advocacy group.

Gabe Roth, the group’s executive director, said he had mixed feelings about Monday’s development.

On the one hand, Roth said the justices should recuse themselves from cases in which they have an economic stake.

On the other, he added, “this is not sustainable.”

It cannot be, he said, that cases involving Bertelsmann and Penguin Random House are immune from Supreme Court review.

Roth has an idea for a fix.

“The justices should place their earnings from book advances and royalties into an account that they can’t touch until they leave the high court,” he said. “Maybe they should be granted some exceptions, like for a home purchase or school tuition for their kids.”

That might solve problems arising from book royalties. But the court has lacked a quorum in other cases, too, including a 2008 appeal brought by more than 50 companies that did business in apartheid-era South Africa.

In that case, Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Samuel Alito and Stephen Breyer were apparently prevented from sitting because of their stock holdings. Justice Anthony Kennedy had a son who worked for one of the companies.

There may be broader solutions. One would be for the justices to focus on their day jobs.

Another would be for Congress to lower the quorum requirement to five. A 1943 editorial in The New York Times floated that idea after the Supreme Court was unable to act in two “cases of high importance” for want of a quorum.

“The court consists of nine members,” the editorial asked. “Why is a majority not a quorum? Why six instead of five?”

The six-justice requirement was an artifact of an era when Congress had briefly increased the size of the court to 10 justices, the editorial said. It suggested new legislation to lower the required number to five.

“If passed, as it should be,” the editorial said, “this will be not merely an apology to insulted mathematics but an end to certain unnecessary delays of justice.”

Please send me your comments on Elon Musk’s money, false friends, the cost of books or anything else at the-docket@nytimes.com. See you next week. — Adam

item.title: Nicole Brown Simpson’s Sister: ‘We Deserve Answers’ on Accomplice Question
item.description:
A sister of Nicole Brown Simpson, the slain ex-wife of O.J. Simpson, said this week that she would like to see law enforcement officials investigate whether multiple people were involved in the 1994 killing.

The sister, Tanya Brown, said she believed someone helped Mr. Simpson get rid of the murder weapon, and highlighted a recent New York Times article that, citing newly unsealed court files and interviews, examined the possibility.

“We deserve answers,” Ms. Brown said.

Ms. Brown Simpson and her friend Ronald Goldman were found stabbed to death in June 1994, and Mr. Simpson was charged with murder. He was acquitted by a Los Angeles County jury in a high-profile criminal trial but later held liable for the deaths in a civil case.

Ms. Brown said she was wary of anything that would fully reopen the case and the trauma of the 1995 trial. But at the same time, she said she would like to see prosecutors seek to answer whether someone helped Mr. Simpson or assisted in a cover-up.

She wasn’t alone in calling for renewed scrutiny of the case.

Alan Dershowitz, one of the lawyers who represented Mr. Simpson, said that a special prosecutor should be appointed to examine whether an accomplice was involved.

Mr. Dershowitz pointed to the findings of The Times’s report, which included documents detailing how a secret informant told law enforcement about the missing murder weapon and Mr. Simpson’s flight from justice. The informant’s brother told The Times that he saw his brother the night of the killings with what appeared to be bloody hands, and that he disposed of a bag with a heavy object inside at his brother’s request.

“The public, even though it’s been 30 years, is entitled to the best evidence as to what really happened or didn’t happen,” said Mr. Dershowitz, a professor emeritus of law at Harvard University.

Another member of the defense team, Robert Blasier, was wary of the idea, given that Mr. Simpson and the informant are now dead. Mr. Blasier, who believes the theories about an accomplice may be true, said that he doubted the world would ever know what really happened.

There are legal hurdles in revisiting the three-decade-old case. In a statement, the Los Angeles County District Attorney’s Office noted that a charge of “accessory after the fact,” used when someone assists a criminal after the crime, carries a three-year statute of limitations. “Under California law, the alleged actions, even if provable, could not be prosecuted due to the lapse of time.”

A spokesman for the Los Angeles Police Department has said that the Simpson case remains “open and ongoing” and that cold case detectives continue to make inquiries as new leads emerge.

In California, the state attorney general and district attorneys can hire or appoint special prosecutors. In Los Angeles there is recent precedent. Nathan Hochman, the district attorney, last year appointed a special prosecutor to investigate police misconduct cases.

During the 1995 murder trial, prosecutors focused on Mr. Simpson as being the lone participant in the murder. More than a decade later, in the book “If I Did It,” Mr. Simpson described a “hypothetical” account in which someone was with him at the scene and then helped him get rid of bloody clothes and the murder weapon.

The secret informant described in the Times article, Joseph Ippolito, had been a mafia associate and convicted drug trafficker from New Jersey who escaped from prison a month before the murders. He was also close friends with Al Cowlings, the confidant of Mr. Simpson who drove the white Bronco during the infamous police chase on the day Mr. Simpson was arrested.

Mr. Ippolito was arrested more than a year after the murders and told federal law enforcement then that he had important information about the state case, including details on the location of the weapon. Federal prosecutors considered Mr. Ippolito “extremely reliable” because he was helping them on successful mafia and drug cases.

Mr. Ippolito had been on the radar of law enforcement officials and even Mr. Simpson’s defense team. But prosecutors in Los Angeles did not seek to bring him in or question him at trial.

Mr. Ippolito died in 2006. Mr. Simpson died in 2024. Mr. Cowlings did not respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Dershowitz said the idea of an accomplice was plausible, as he from the start had wondered about the missing murder weapon.

“I’ve often thought that there might have been an accomplice,” Mr. Dershowitz said.

Laurie Levenson, a professor at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles who commented on the Simpson case at the time, said she doubted a special prosecutor would be appointed and questioned whether it would lead to a break in the case. She is doubtful any new evidence could emerge.

Still, she faulted the authorities in Los Angeles for, in her view, not thoroughly investigating what Mr. Cowlings may have known about the killings.

“I think this is a bit like the Jimmy Hoffa story,” she said. “It will keep going because it was never resolved.”

item.title: Key Trump Health Adviser Resigns Ahead of Midterm Elections
item.description:
Calley Means, a leader of the Make America Healthy Again movement, resigned from the Trump administration on Thursday, signaling a further erosion of a coalition that helped propel President Trump to power a second time.

Mr. Means, a top adviser at the Department of Health and Human Services, was a key official behind policies around food quality, including an effort to increase disclosure of the chemicals in food, remove artificial food dyes and ban soda from the federal food assistance program known as SNAP.

He also worked on an executive order to support the development of psychedelic medications, which got a boost from the podcast host Joe Rogan.

“I leave with tremendous respect for President Trump and R.F.K. Jr. — two historic figures who are committed to confronting a corrupt D.C. bureaucracy that is doing everything possible to protect the status quo,” Mr. Means said in a statement.

In recent months, though, he began to feel stymied in his attempts to deliver on promises to improve the food supply, such as by defining ultraprocessed foods, an initial step to regulating them, according to a person close to him.

Vani Hari, a MAHA leader and healthy eating influencer, said that a turning point for Mr. Means came when the White House roiled the MAHA movement with an executive order supporting the increased production of glyphosate, a pesticide that the movement is particularly focused on eliminating.

“It became very clear in the last few months that no progress was getting made,” she said. “And when you’re spinning around in circles, you can only take so much.”

Mr. Means’s profile rose before he joined the administration, during a podcast tour on which he decried the manipulative tactics of lobbyists from his experience with the beverage industry. He continued to view lobbyists as a corrupting force in Washington, said Ms. Hari.

“Calley was the architect of MAHA,” Ms. Hari said. “He was one of the most successful food policy advocates in history, in my opinion, at this point. And it’s a sad day for the U.S. government to lose him.”

Mr. Means, who was a campaign adviser to Mr. Kennedy and Mr. Trump, played a key role in brokering their agreement to join forces in the final months of the 2024 campaign.

After Mr. Trump was shot in the ear during a rally in Butler, Pa., in July 2024, Mr. Kennedy spoke about wanting to offer support, given his family’s history of tragic political violence. Mr. Means encouraged Mr. Kennedy to call the president, starting what would become a running dialogue.

Their alliance has been credited with helping Mr. Trump win the White House again, given the support of voters who embraced a message of pushback on corporations to protect children from a toxic food supply.

The administration quickly secured agreements from food companies that pledged to remove artificial dyes and seed oils from their products. Mr. Means also played a key role in MAHA reports outlining goals to reduce chronic disease in children. He worked on other initiatives to require nutrition education in medical school, and on a revised food pyramid.

Mr. Means has shown little interest in Mr. Kennedy’s work on vaccines, finding it to be a polarizing topic. He has preferred to see Mr. Kennedy focus more on the healthy eating part of his agenda.

Before his work on the presidential campaigns, Mr. Means cowrote a book with Casey Means, his sister. They argued that people could avoid chronic disease through careful attention to diet, exercise and some less conventional efforts, such as monitoring glucose levels.

Mr. Trump last year nominated Ms. Means to be the surgeon general, but withdrew her from consideration when it became clear that she did not have enough Senate votes for confirmation.

Mr. Means also ran Truemed, the company he co-founded, for most of his first year at the Department of Health and Human Services, advising on an array of health topics while holding a significant stake in a company. The company offered a marketplace of items people could buy with health savings account funds, which were opened to additional people under a policy that Mr. Trump enacted in 2025.

In the administration, Mr. Means could be outspoken and direct, and was a pugnacious profile on social media, castigating critics. In recent days, his frustration became apparent in his posts on one of his signature issues — the health effects of ultraprocessed food consumption, which he said was “highly tied to our chronic disease crisis that is killing Americans and bankrupting our country.”

Still, he wrote in his resignation statement that “the past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and health care incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started.”

item.title: Jeffries Plans Final Midterm Sprint Through Battleground Districts
item.description:
Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, is set to campaign in the lower Hudson Valley on Saturday with the Democrat running to flip one of the country’s most competitive seats. The visit kicks off his final sprint through the swing districts that will decide whether his party can win control of the House.

Mr. Jeffries will appear with Cait Conley, a combat veteran who served in Iraq and Afghanistan. She is running to unseat Representative Mike Lawler, a two-term Republican whose signature policy victory, raising the cap on state and local tax deductions, has been popular across party lines.

Mr. Jeffries is also planning to campaign in the coming days in Republican-leaning districts in San Antonio, Texas, and Omaha, Neb.; competitive districts in Virginia Beach, San Diego and Orange County that Democrats are pushing to flip; and the hotly contested Long Island district held by Representative Tom Suozzi, a Democrat.

That Mr. Jeffries is welcome and wanted in battleground districts underscores these candidates’ view of him as a broadly appealing enough surrogate who can help make a pitch that resonates with their voters. It is a contrast to how former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, long vilified by the right as an extreme partisan, operated on the campaign trail, where many centrist Democrats needed to distance themselves from her.

And it serves as a reminder that even in a year when much of the energy among Democrats has been captured by candidates further to the left, the party’s chances of taking the House majority — and Mr. Jeffries’s chance to become speaker — are in the hands of more moderate candidates running in competitive areas.

During the 2018 midterm election cycle, Republicans sought to tarnish Democrats running in swing districts by tying them to Ms. Pelosi, capitalizing on their yearslong campaign to demonize and dehumanize her.

That year, many Democrats in tough races said they would not support her for speaker. This year, Republicans have tried to brand Democrats as “socialists,” casting the stars of the left, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, in the role of boogeyman.

They rarely mention Mr. Jeffries, a more neutral figure and an establishment Democrat who has led his party in the House since 2022.

“He’s not seen as a figure of the left,” said David Axelrod, a Democratic strategist. “That’s reflected in the fact that unlike the president himself, he’s getting invited to competitive places in order to campaign.”

Mr. Axelrod added, “There’s no voter in America who is saying, ‘I don’t want my representative associating with Hakeem Jeffries.’”

A group of young, anti-establishment candidates who have won primaries in heavily Democratic districts this year have refused to pledge their support for Mr. Jeffries, who in many ways embodies a party firmament from which they are looking to break.

Should Democrats win the House, managing the insurgent left could emerge as one of his biggest challenges as speaker. But for now, he is seen as an asset in the critical districts that would give him a majority.

For Mr. Jeffries, the stop on Saturday in the Hudson Valley is also personal.

He harbors a particular aversion to Mr. Lawler, who last year showily confronted him in the Capitol, in front of reporters and news cameras, during the government shutdown.

“My constituents are suffering as a result of your ridiculous ploy,” Mr. Lawler told Mr. Jeffries during a five-minute confrontation, punctuated by repeated use of the term “bro,” in which both men shouted in each other’s faces.

“Listen, you’re a complete and total embarrassment right now,” Mr. Jeffries told Mr. Lawler. “Is this supposed to be a video for your failed re-election? Is that what’s going on right now?”

Since the heated encounter, Mr. Jeffries has referred to Mr. Lawler as an “irrelevant individual” and an “unadulterated phony” who has never crossed party lines on a vote that mattered.

In a statement, Mr. Jeffries said that Ms. Conley was “going to defeat partisan hack Mike Lawler in November, and retire one of Donald Trump’s biggest allies in Congress.” He has said that the race will be the one he is watching most closely on election night.

Last cycle, Democrats flipped a number of competitive New York seats, electing Representatives Laura Gillen, Josh Riley and John W. Mannion in seats once held by Republicans. Mr. Suozzi flipped his seat in a special election.

But Mr. Lawler held on.

The district has posed a particular challenge for Democrats. Nearly a third of voters there are unaffiliated, and roughly half of households include an emergency medical worker, law enforcement officer or veteran.

Recent polls have found the race almost tied. Ms. Conley is leading Mr. Lawler, 48 to 46 percent, according to a recent Emerson College poll.

Spencer Kimball, the executive director of Emerson College Polling, noted that two years ago in a poll at the same time in the race, 20 percent of Democrats in the district supported Mr. Lawler. This time, that support has fallen to 12 percent. Republican support for the Democratic candidate, meanwhile, has risen to 10 percent from 4 percent.

Mr. Lawler, for his part, has attempted to frame himself as a pragmatic and independent Republican who works with Democrats. He proudly points out that President Trump called him a “pain in the ass” for pushing for those tax deductions. Representative Jared Golden, the Maine Democrat who is retiring, recently endorsed him.

item.title: Justice Dept. Opens Inquiry Into Corey Lewandowski
item.description:
The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation into Corey Lewandowski over accusations that he personally profited from his role as a top adviser to the Department of Homeland Security, according to two officials with knowledge of the situation.

The inquiry, one of the rare instances in which an ally or appointee of President Trump’s has been investigated for potential wrongdoing during his second term, is in response to a referral from the Department of Homeland Security’s inspector general, those officials said.

It was not immediately clear what actions are under investigation.

A lawyer for Mr. Lewandowski forcefully pushed back against any suggestion of criminal activity. “Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” the lawyer, Adam Trigg, said in a statement.

The Wall Street Journal earlier reported news of the inquiry.

Mr. Lewandowski, who served as Mr. Trump’s first campaign manager a decade ago, worked closely with Kristi Noem, the former homeland security secretary, but left after she was forced out in March.

After Ms. Noem left the Department of Homeland Security, she took on a role as a special envoy for Western Hemisphere security at the State Department. But her term was not renewed when it ended in September. She now holds a lower-profile role as a senior adviser at the State Department.

The catalyst for Ms. Noem’s firing appeared to be her answers during two congressional hearings, particularly her under-threat-of-perjury statements that Mr. Trump had approved of tens of millions of dollars of government ads in which she was prominently featured.

Mr. Lewandowski wielded power far beyond the scope of his role as an unpaid adviser, serving as Ms. Noem’s top aide and confidant. He often hosted meetings in her office without her present, grilling agency officials and issuing orders as he flexed his vast influence over Mr. Trump’s efforts to detain and deport millions of immigrants.

While he joined the department early last year in what was supposed to be a limited, part-time role, Mr. Lewandowski, a longtime Republican operative, used his perch to build an expansive portfolio in which he had wide influence over personnel, contracts and department operations.

Mr. Lewandowski helped elevate Gregory Bovino, a midlevel leader of the U.S. Border Patrol, to a senior position commanding militarized deportation raids across the United States.

Mr. Bovino was forced out earlier this year after agents under his supervision killed two protesters in Minneapolis during an aggressive immigration sweep that he oversaw.

In the last hours of Ms. Noem’s tenure, her agency delivered a windfall to one of her political donors by buying five airplanes from the man’s firm at a substantial markup.

The Department of Homeland Security agreed to pay the donor’s firm $108 million for a Boeing 737 airliner that had been converted into a huge private jet, complete with a stand-up bar, two bedrooms, marble showers and a table covered in manta ray skin.

The firm, Daedalus Aviation Corporation, had bought the same plane a few months earlier from a seller who had asked for less than $90 million, according to documents reviewed by The New York Times.

Alan Feuer, Maggie Haberman and Hamed Aleaziz contributed reporting.

item.title: Florida Police Officer Is Accused in Scheme to Seize a Dead Man’s House
item.description:
On July 11, 2022, Officer Brian Sguros and a partner responded to a call for a welfare check on a 71-year-old man who lived alone in a blue two-story house on a side street in Lauderhill, Fla. A neighbor reported that she had not seen the man, Dennis I. West, in about two weeks.

After arriving at the house in that city north of Miami, the officers found Mr. West’s decomposed body lying face up near the door, with no signs of any forced entry or crime. Everything proceeded routinely from there: The house was boarded up and the medical examiner determined that Mr. West had died of cardiovascular disease.

What happened over the next three years was anything but routine. According to the Broward County Sheriff’s Office, Officer Sguros, a member of the Lauderhill Police Department, proceeded to use Mr. West’s identity as part of a complex scheme to take control of the house, even though Mr. West had living relatives who should have inherited the property.

Officer Sguros, 35, was arrested on Tuesday and charged with official misconduct, criminal use of a deceased person’s identification, criminal use of personal identification information, offense against a computer user and unlawful use of a two-way communication device, the sheriff’s office said.

Officer Sguros did not respond to a text message on Thursday, and it wasn’t immediately clear if he had a lawyer. The Lauderhill Police Department said he had been placed on administrative leave without pay.

“Every officer in this department swears an oath to protect the people of Lauderhill, including those who can no longer speak for themselves,” the city’s police chief, Constance Stanley, said in a statement.

One of Mr. West’s brothers, Gary West, said he was appalled by the allegations.

“It’s a terrible thing for someone to do,” he said in an interview on Thursday. “If you can’t trust a police officer, who the hell can you trust?”

According to the sheriff’s office, Officer Sguros became involved in Mr. West’s affairs soon after discovering his body.

He told the medical examiner in Broward County that he was Mr. West’s friend, although there is no indication that he knew Mr. West, court records show. He also told the medical examiner that Mr. West had no living relatives and that he was willing to handle funeral arrangements, the records show.

In September 2022, Officer Sguros signed paperwork authorizing the medical examiner to release Mr. West’s body for cremation.

Marty Kiar, the Broward County property appraiser, said that investigators believed that Mr. West was cremated but they were still trying to find out what happened to his ashes.

According to court filings, Officer Sguros then began to repair Mr. West’s house, a 1,900-square-foot property with an attached garage that was built in the 1960s.

He paid the utility bills and property taxes and, by his own account, spent at least $214,000 on renovations to increase the property value. Broward County records indicate the house is now worth $403,590.

A neighbor said in court filings that after Mr. West died, she noticed work had been done on the lighting and air conditioning at the home and that the swimming pool had been covered. She also remembered chatting with a uniformed police officer outside the house and being happy that an officer was moving into the neighborhood.

In February 2025, Officer Sguros filed a formal legal notice to begin the process of claiming ownership of the property.

In a sworn statement in that case, Officer Sguros acknowledged that he had found Mr. West’s body and said that he “took possession” of the house in August 2022. At the time, he said, it was “uninhabitable” and filled with trash and debris. Its roof had partially collapsed and the swimming pool had been “left as an open pit,” he said.

A few months after Officer Sguros filed that legal notice, a realty company noticed it and discovered the house was associated with Mr. West. It located Mr. West’s living relatives, who include his two brothers, and paid them for the property.

But the company found that Officer Sguros was in possession of the house and contacted the Lauderhill Police Department, Mr. Kiar said. As the company prepared to take legal action against the officer, he surrendered the keys to the house, court records show.

Broward County investigators then dug into the case. They discovered that, in 2024, an application for a permit to repair the exterior doors and windows of Mr. West’s home appeared to have been filed by Mr. West, even though he had died two years earlier, court records show.

The paperwork listed Officer Sguros’s phone number as the contact, but it had Mr. West listed as the property owner, court records show. It also contained information from Mr. West’s Florida driver’s license and a signature that purported to be Mr. West’s, the sheriff’s office said. It said the detective overseeing the investigation believed Officer Sguros “forged West’s signature on the permit.”

Mr. Kiar said the case was unique among the hundreds of property crimes his office has investigated in South Florida, which he called “the title fraud capital of the world.”

“This is the first time that I can think of that someone in law enforcement is alleged to have done this, and that’s what makes this so concerning,” Mr. Kiar said, adding that the allegations represented “a true breach of the public trust.”

item.title: Bard College Hired Forensic Firm to Investigate a Damning Epstein Email
item.description:
After a congressman highlighted an explosive email apparently sent from Bard College’s former president to the convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, the school jumped into action.

It hired a cybersecurity forensic firm to examine whether the email was real. The company quickly turned around a report on Monday suggesting it could be fake.

Some congressional Democrats were incredulous, saying the email might simply have been deleted and that the firm’s analysis did not explain why or how someone might have manufactured the message.

In it, someone writing from the Bard president’s email address asks Mr. Epstein whether a young woman was “for me, or are you keeping her for yourself.”

The contention over the email is the latest, and perhaps most intense, dispute over the former Bard president’s ties to Mr. Epstein. Leon Botstein, the longtime president of the small liberal-arts college, retired over the summer amid the scrutiny, although he remained in several Bard positions.

He stepped away from all of them this month, on the same day that Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, sent a scathing letter to Bard highlighting the message about a young woman.

For his part, Dr. Botstein welcomed the report from the cybersecurity forensic firm. “As I previously said, I did not author or send that email,” he said in a statement. “I appreciate the effort to find the truth.”

That email, dated May 2014, concerns a young foreign model and aspiring vocalist who Mr. Raskin suggests was being groomed and trafficked by Mr. Epstein. In his letter, the congressman wrote that Mr. Epstein used his relationship with Dr. Botstein, who is also the principal conductor of the American Symphony Orchestra, to convince the woman she could have a successful music career.

Bard said it was reviewing the claims in Mr. Raskin’s letter, which included other allegations against the president, including that he played an improper role in how sexual misconduct cases on campus were handled. It also immediately hired the cybersecurity firm, FTI Consulting, to investigate the authenticity of the message to Mr. Epstein.

Twelve days later, the firm issued its report.

The email was not the original, but was in a message Mr. Epstein forwarded to himself, making it harder to analyze, the firm noted. Mr. Epstein often forwarded emails and news articles to himself, including in some instances where he kept potentially embarrassing or incriminating information about people in his orbit.

The firm said it could not find the 2014 email stored in Bard’s email system. The firm also found discrepancies in the date and formats that the investigators suggested might point to tampering, though it could not say so definitively.

FTI did not answer questions about its report or about how someone might have manufactured the disputed message. Bard declined to comment beyond its statement.

Democrats on the House committee released a sharp response, questioning the firm’s methods and conclusions. Among other things, they pointed out that the email could have been deleted or lost.

“The report also raises a vague claim that the email could have been manipulated without explaining why Epstein would forge an email incriminating himself,” Nelly Decker, a spokeswoman for House Judiciary Democrats, said in a statement.

Matthew Green, a cryptography expert at Johns Hopkins University who reviewed the FTI report at The Times’s request, said that the messages “don’t really look right.”

“They do look like someone might have hand written the dates,” Dr. Green said. “That doesn’t prove that all of the text was forged, but I think there’s something unusual about them.”

A trove of records released earlier this year by the Justice Department showed a friendly correspondence between Dr. Botstein and Mr. Epstein that lasted for years. Dr. Botstein signed off one message “Miss you,” and sent supportive notes to the convicted sex offender after negative media coverage. Dr. Botstein also visited Mr. Epstein, even planning a trip to his island in 2012.

Dr. Botstein, known as a talented fund-raiser who kept the once financially struggling liberal arts college afloat, has consistently maintained that the sole purpose of his relationship with Mr. Epstein was to convince him to give a major donation to Bard — money that never materialized.

Among the many messages the men sent each other, Dr. Botstein has only questioned the authenticity of the one highlighted by the congressman.

Dr. Botstein’s critics have painted the message as a smoking gun, suggesting that he may have abetted or even taken part in Mr. Epstein’s abuse. Mr. Raskin’s letter said it was hard to construct an innocent explanation for the question, which he noted was asked to “the most famous sexual predator of our time.”

It appears the report won’t end scrutiny of the message and Dr. Botstein’s broader relationship with Mr. Epstein. Ms. Decker said in her statement that the judiciary committee has requested all emails between Dr. Botstein and Mr. Epstein to determine “the full extent of his culpability.”

In a statement, Bard said it would continue to examine the allegations, while working “to provide a secure and respectful learning environment for everyone at Bard.”

item.title: What Dueling Visits by Ocasio-Cortez and Manchin Say About Maine’s Senate Race
item.description:
In the final stage of the tight Senate race in Maine, Senator Susan Collins, a Republican, is trying to shore up her support in the center. Troy Jackson, her progressive Democratic challenger, is trying to excite his party’s base.

Their contrasting strategies were on display across two days this week in a race that could determine control of the Senate.

On Thursday, Mr. Jackson, wearing a button-down shirt under a navy vest, appeared at a theater in the state’s largest city, joined by Representative Alexandria-Ocasio Cortez of New York, a 37-year-old democratic socialist who is considering a run for president. The visit followed trips by Senators Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren, two progressive leaders, to Maine to back Mr. Jackson.

On Wednesday, Ms. Collins, clad in a light blue suit, joined a 79-year-old retired senator with centrist credentials, former Senator Joe Manchin III of West Virginia, a former Democrat, for low-key stops at a century-old diner and a dusty shoe factory in politically split regions.

“I’m not A.O.C.,” Mr. Manchin said with a grin.

The two days of campaigning offered hints of where each side believes it has work to do in the electorate with less than two weeks left until Election Day. And they underscored the choice facing Maine voters.

They can side for a sixth straight election with Ms. Collins, who has long maintained a hold on a Democratic-leaning state by burnishing a reputation as a Republican who can work with Democrats. Or they can chart a new course, backing a progressive Democrat who has railed against the Trump administration and cast Ms. Collins as an enabler of the president.

Ms. Collins is trying to reassert her hold on an independent-minded electorate while arguing that Mr. Jackson is too far left for her state, which has one of the country’s oldest populations. Mr. Jackson, a former State Senate president, is working to activate the state’s many Democratic and Democratic-leaning voters who say they are hungry for change and infuriated by the Trump administration and Republicans who have supported it.

Ms. Collins, 73, in her understated style, questioned Mr. Jackson’s decision to bring Ms. Ocasio-Cortez to Maine — and noted that it came less than two weeks after Mr. Jackson, 58, campaigned with Mr. Sanders of Vermont.

Ms. Collins told reporters at the New Balance factory in Norway, Maine, on Wednesday that Mr. Jackson “certainly has every right to invite whomever he wants to campaign with him in Maine.” But, she added, “So far, it’s been from the far left of the party.”

On Thursday afternoon, Mr. Jackson appeared with Ms. Ocasio-Cortez at a nearly 2,000-seat theater in deep-blue and voter-rich Portland.

The congresswoman told the crowd that there were “a lot of consultants” who would advise Mr. Jackson not to campaign with her. “It takes a lot to say, you know what, no, I know my people, and I know who I am, and I’m going to do things my way,” she said. “So thank you, Troy.”

Mr. Jackson said Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was “exactly what I want in my government — somebody that’s not afraid to stand up, fight for what she believes in.”

A runner-up in the Democratic primary for Maine governor this year, Mr. Jackson in July secured the Senate nomination as the choice of the state party’s left wing — replacing another progressive, Graham Platner, who initially won the nomination but left the race after a rape allegation, which he denied.

Mr. Jackson’s recent appearances are aimed at exciting younger and more progressive voters. A New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena poll last month suggested that Mr. Jackson held a narrower lead with young voters than other Democrats running this cycle. And some Maine Democrats say they are worried that Mr. Jackson has not excited the party’s base the way Mr. Platner did during the primary.

Ms. Collins has been facing an avalanche of attacks from Democrats, who have cast her as an ally of Mr. Trump and have hammered her over her vote to confirm a Supreme Court justice, Brett M. Kavanaugh, who helped overturn Roe v. Wade. Ms. Collins, in turn, has been trying to remind voters of times she has worked with Democrats and broken on key issues with the president, whom she has never voted for, according to her campaign.

James Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington, said Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s visit carried more risk and more potential reward than Mr. Manchin’s, because the congresswoman could both “fire up” Democrats and put off some conservatives.

“A.O.C.’s appearance could have more effect than Manchin’s,” he said. “But it cuts both ways.”

item.title: Supreme Court Allows Blanket Ban on Student IDs at Polls in New Hampshire
item.description:
The Supreme Court agreed on Thursday that New Hampshire can direct election officials not to consider student IDs when verifying voters’ identities, ahead of the midterm elections.

New Hampshire’s secretary of state in April ordered officials to avoid reviewing student IDs, even in conjunction with other documents, for voters who are having trouble establishing their identity when checking in at the polls or requesting absentee ballots.

Republican state leaders had argued that the measure was needed to combat voter fraud and had asked the Supreme Court to intervene after a lower court blocked the directive earlier this month.

The ruling by the court did not include a vote count, which is typical for such emergency orders. The one-paragraph order explained the court’s reasoning by quoting a previous Supreme Court ruling that said the justices have “repeatedly emphasized” that “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, writing that she viewed the federal judge’s action as merely a “targeted order” to correct public statements and guidance by the state’s secretary of state that the lower court judge had concluded were “at best, misleading.”

The ruling dealt with a relatively rare circumstance in New Hampshire — how election officials exercise their discretion when a voter has difficulty verifying their identity. It is not clear how many voters will be affected by the court’s action. Still, the dispute was symbolic of the lengths to which both sides have gone in battles over voter identification ahead of the hotly contested vote.

The retirement of Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a long-serving Democrat, set off a high-stakes contest for an open Senate seat in New Hampshire, making it an important battleground. Democratic candidate Chris Pappas is running against former Senator John E. Sununu, a Republican, in a race that both parties view as critical.

The ruling was the latest in a string of election-related emergency actions by the justices in the lead-up to November, including their blocking of a Trump plan to screen ballots sent through the postal system, which would have drastically altered how Americans vote by mail.

More issues are expected to reach the justices before, and potentially after, the Nov. 3 vote.

The New Hampshire challenge stems from a law signed in April by Gov. Kelly Ayotte that required government-issued identification like a driver’s license or passport to vote. It prevented voters from using student IDs as the sole method of proving their identities at the polls.

After the measure was signed, Secretary of State David Scanlan, who oversees elections in New Hampshire, issued a directive that student IDs could not be used under any circumstances.

Republicans had asserted that the law was needed to eliminate the possibility that someone could present a fake college ID card at the polls. Democrats countered that it was a tactic to make it harder for young people to vote, arguing that high school and college students who do not have driver’s licenses might struggle to find other ways to prove their identities.

New Hampshire has required voters to show identification since 2012. In 2024, the state tightened its rules, eliminating some exceptions to rules that require photo identification and requiring first-time voters to present a birth certificate, passport or other official citizenship document to register.

Voter advocacy groups challenged the student ID law, arguing that it violated the Constitution and would disenfranchise hundreds, possibly thousands, of qualified voters.

They also argued that the secretary of state’s directive went too far, asserting that under a “safety valve” provision in state law, if a voter is unable to prove their identity by a document listed in the statute, election officials should be able to consider a student ID as evidence to help prove the voter’s identity.

In a ruling earlier this month, a federal judge declined to pause the New Hampshire law for the midterms but blocked the directive that student IDs could not be used under the “safety valve” provision. The judge found that the state had “offered no independent justification for that broader prohibition.”

In asking the justices to weigh in, New Hampshire state officials argued that the lower court had injected “uncertainty” into the state’s election procedures. State officials had already distributed student voting guides and launched a public campaign to explain how the voter ID law worked. They asserted that the judge’s decision would require state officials to “reverse all these efforts in the immediate lead-up to the general election.”

The Republican National Committee weighed in to support the New Hampshire voting rules, arguing that the judge’s decision “threatens to disrupt identity verification in New Hampshire’s looming elections.”

In response, the voter advocacy groups argued that it was Republicans who were attempting to inject uncertainty into the election by changing the rules “in the direction that keeps eligible voters from proving who they are.”

item.title: Bernie Sanders Gives $1 Million to Bolster El-Sayed and Counter AIPAC in Michigan
item.description:
Senator Bernie Sanders was so irate when he learned on Wednesday that the nation’s top pro-Israel lobby planned to spend as much as $9 million to defeat Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee in Michigan’s Senate race, that he immediately transferred $1 million to him.

Then Mr. Sanders and his team started making calls.

They dialed other progressive allies, urging them to pony up to counter the spending from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee to help elect Dr. El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim senator in American history.

“What I have done today was not only put a million into Abdul’s campaign, but we are also reaching out to other individuals to try to raise money because this is just outrageous,” Mr. Sanders, the 85-year-old independent from Vermont, said in an interview.

By the end of day on Wednesday, the Sanders operation had collected promises and pledges totaling $300,000 from a dozen other Democrats, including Senators Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, Tina Smith of Minnesota, Chris Van Hollen of Maryland and Jeff Merkley of Oregon, according to a list provided by Mr. Sanders’s team.

“That’s nowhere near what AIPAC is doing,” Mr. Sanders said. “It’s nowhere near what other super PACs — billionaire-funded super PACs — are doing. But it is a way to stand with democracy and with Abdul’s campaign.”

Mr. Sanders had already given the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund — a joint effort of Dr. El-Sayed’s campaign, the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and the Michigan Democratic State Central Committee — $250,000 in the first week of October. The elder progressive had $22.4 million in his campaign coffers entering October, among the largest sums for a sitting senator.

The New York Times reported on Wednesday that AIPAC was making a rare decision to invest in a Republican in a general election, contributing as much as $9 million to a super PAC supporting Mike Rogers, a former congressman and the Republican nominee.

Mr. Rogers had opened the door to AIPAC’s support in an Oct. 8 debate, saying he would “take all of that help.” AIPAC has not commented on its spending.

Mr. Sanders is not the only big-name progressive who has added to Dr. El-Sayed’s finances this month in a race being watched nationwide. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York donated $1 million while campaigning with him in Michigan last week.

Mr. Sanders has been fighting with AIPAC for years over the direction of the Democratic Party. In the 2022 midterms, he told The Times, “This is a war for the future of the Democratic Party.”

The disdain appears to be mutual.

After Mr. Sanders wrote in a post on social media on Thursday that “AIPAC is why we’re at war in Iran,” the organization delivered a tongue-in-cheek response.

“AIPAC is why your fantasy football team stinks,” the main AIPAC account wrote on X. “AIPAC is why the weather is bad. AIPAC is why you need an app to park. Say NO to Bernie’s obsessive scapegoating.”

Mr. Sanders did not care for the phrase.

“No, this is not Bernie Sanders’s obsessive scapegoating,” Mr. Sanders said. “This is a fact.”

Referring to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, he added, “The fact is, the American people do not want to continue spending billions of dollars on Netanyahu’s extremist government.”

On Wednesday, Dr. El-Sayed called Representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington, the chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, after The Times reported the coming AIPAC spending.

“Can you help?” he asked her, Ms. Jayapal recalled.

Her leadership PAC had given $350,000 to support Dr. El-Sayed in the primary, and she said she was reviewing how much more she could help now. She called for Senator Gary Peters, the retiring Democrat whose seat Dr. El-Sayed is seeking, to chip in, too.

“I think he’s got $7 or 8 million in his bank account — I’d love to see him come in with $1 million as well,” she said. “I think we need to see moderate and establishment Democrats be as committed to the party rallying around the nominee as they are when we get flak for progressives not rallying around a nominee.”

The office of Mr. Peters did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

item.title: Omar Case Could Hinge on Her Birth Date, but She Says No Records Exist
item.description:
A federal investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar’s immigration history could depend in part on proving when she was born. But irrefutable records of her birth date might be difficult or even impossible to obtain because the Minnesota Democrat spent her early years in war-torn Somalia and a Kenyan refugee camp.

President Trump and members of his administration have long asserted that Ms. Omar, a frequent critic of the president, committed immigration fraud. Last week, in an extraordinary escalation of those claims, federal agents searched her Washington-area house.

The government has not released any public documents providing insight into its evidence. But top administration officials have suggested that Ms. Omar, who came to the United States as a child more than three decades ago, could ultimately lose her citizenship.

Scrutiny of Ms. Omar’s birth date intensified after she sought years ago to have the year of her birth adjusted in some sources. She said she was correcting inaccurate listings, but critics have called the changes suspicious.

Ms. Omar has said she obtained citizenship through her late father as a minor, but if she is actually one year older than she maintains, she may have been ineligible for the citizenship.

Ms. Omar has adamantly denied having committed immigration fraud and called the investigation an abuse of power.

Here is what to know about this case:

Ms. Omar’s office said she was born on Oct. 4, 1982, in Mogadishu, Somalia. She fled her homeland as it descended into civil war in the early 1990s. She, her father and six siblings escaped “flying bullets overhead and starvation-level food shortages” before arriving at a refugee camp in Kenya, she wrote in a memoir.

Ms. Omar and her relatives were admitted to the United States as refugees in 1995. After initially settling in Arlington, Va., they moved to Minneapolis, home to the largest Somali diaspora in the United States.

Refugees can become eligible to apply for citizenship five years after their arrival. Ms. Omar has said she acquired citizenship through her father’s naturalization case in 2000, when she was 17.

This claim appears to be central to the investigation into Ms. Omar.

Weeks before the search of Ms. Omar’s home on Oct. 12, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative commentator that investigators examining her family immigration history had found “some illegal activity for them to come to the United States to begin with.” Mr. Mullin added, “If we can prove that you shouldn’t have been here in the first place, we’ll deport you.”

Several people familiar with the case told The New York Times that investigators were exploring whether Ms. Omar was actually 18, and not a minor, when she became a U.S. citizen. If she was an adult, she would have been ineligible for the so-called derivative citizenship.

Investigators are also looking at whether Ms. Omar’s late father lied or omitted information in immigration forms before becoming a U.S. citizen, and whether family members have since conspired to conceal information that may have jeopardized their immigration petitions, according to the people familiar with the case.

Several members of Ms. Omar’s family, including a sister, Sahra Noor, have received subpoenas directing them to appear before a federal grand jury in Minnesota. Such subpoenas allow prosecutors to question people under oath as grand jurors assess whether there is enough evidence to hand down an indictment.

Ms. Omar’s immigration history has been investigated by federal authorities for over a decade, but those inquiries have not led to charges.

The current investigation is being overseen by Justice Department leaders, who have faced extraordinary pressure from the White House to prosecute critics of Mr. Trump.

The president has long expressed disdain for Ms. Omar. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump told reporters that Ms. Omar could face deportation, calling her a “sick and very dishonest person.”

Starting last year, senior members of his administration began hinting that her immigration paperwork was being scrutinized. In March, Vice President JD Vance said he was certain that Ms. Omar had committed immigration fraud.

People familiar with the case said that this year, officials seized a phone belonging to Ms. Noor, the sister. The phone contained family text messages about immigration matters, according to the people familiar with the case.

Immigrants approved for naturalization can automatically extend their newly acquired citizenship to children under 18. To qualify for this type of citizenship, minors must be permanent residents living in the United States in the legal custody of the naturalizing parent.

Minors eligible for derivative citizenship are issued a certificate of citizenship, which can be used to get a passport. Those who are 18 or older do not qualify for this type of bundled citizenship and must file stand-alone applications.

Ms. Omar’s office says she was born in 1982. But in the past, her birth year was listed as 1981 in some sources, including the reference library of the Minnesota Legislature, where Ms. Omar served as a lawmaker for two years starting in 2017.

Her birth year was updated at the request of Ms. Omar’s congressional staff in 2019, David Schmidtke, the deputy director of the Minnesota legislative library, said in an email. “We do not have supporting documentation, as the information was self-reported,” he said.

Ms. Omar does not have a birth certificate or a similar vital record that would conclusively show when she was born, according to Jackie Rogers, her spokeswoman. Ms. Rogers called the 1981 birth date references clerical errors.

Somalis who fled their country’s civil war often arrived in refugee camps without birth certificates or other vital records, said Muna Saleh, a professor at Ohio State University who studies Somali resettlement in the United States. Many older immigrants and people from rural areas never had birth records to begin with, she said. Several buildings that contained vital records were destroyed during the war.

Many refugees who came to the United States had only a travel document issued by the United Nations refugee agency. Because many did not know their birth date, U.N. personnel often listed it as Jan. 1 by default.

For many refugees, U.N. travel documents became the underlying source for identity documents issued at various stages of the immigration process in the United States, said Dr. Saleh, who called the investigation into Ms. Omar’s immigration highly unusual.

“We don’t see cases where decades later the government invests so many resources to pick apart the story of a person’s journey to the United States,” she said.

A Supreme Court case from the 1960s established that, with narrow exceptions, the government can only revoke a person’s citizenship if it was obtained through fraud or despite omission of key facts.

If the government concludes that the lawmaker was ineligible to become a citizen in 2000, it would have a few options, according to immigration lawyers.

Officials could pursue a denaturalization case in federal court, where a judge would decide whether the evidence warrants revoking her citizenship. Alternatively, the government could nullify Ms. Omar’s certificate of citizenship and passport, a move Ms. Omar could challenge in court. The government could also place Ms. Omar in deportation proceedings in immigration court, where she could assert that she is a citizen.

In a court filing this week, federal prosecutors referred to Ms. Omar by a different name, Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, and suggested the one she uses is an alias. The government has not explained its basis for doing that.

People familiar with the investigation have said it involved a possible conspiracy, but it’s not clear how many people are under criminal investigation or what charges they could face.

The warrant used to search Ms. Omar’s home was supported by an affidavit by a federal agent laying out why the government believed searching her home could yield evidence of a crime. News organizations have asked a judge to make that document public. Unless it is unsealed or unless charges are filed, the public may not get a detailed understanding of the scope and nature of the investigation.

Alan Feuer contributed reporting.

item.title: The Ad Dividing the Republican Party
item.description:
Twelve days before the midterms, President Trump seems to have a question for his party.

Do you support Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad against his Democratic rival, or are you a RINO?

This week, Ramaswamy, the Republican nominee for governor in Ohio, released a jaw-dropping television ad: a direct-to-camera appeal from the mother of Dr. Amy Acton, who has been estranged from her daughter for decades, calling her daughter a liar and urging people not to vote for her.

The ad has prompted a geyser of criticism from Ramaswamy’s own party and led Trump and Vice President JD Vance to dig in on his behalf, reopening a larger divide among Republicans — one that has been playing out in Ohio for years — at a moment when many would have preferred to maintain a united front.

It also sets up one more big question for Nov. 3: More than a decade into the Trump era, can scorched-earth politics still backfire?

Acton is the former director of the Ohio Department of Health, and she and Ramaswamy are locked in a contentious and remarkably tight race, given Ohio’s Republican leanings.

She hasn’t seen or spoken to her mother since 1978, the year that her stepfather was charged with raping her. She was 12 then, and she later told an Ohio newspaper that the abuse had gone on for three years. Her mother supported her stepfather, not Acton.

The attack ad did not directly raise the allegations of molestation, but it deployed an unspeakably painful family history as a workaday political weapon, as Acton’s mother charged that her daughter had lied about her difficult upbringing.

The ad has been roundly denounced by a slew of Republicans, from the former South Carolina governor Nikki Haley to, remarkably, Gov. Mike DeWine of Ohio — the man who has the job Ramaswamy is hoping to get. DeWine this morning called it “deeply, deeply troubling.”

This afternoon, Trump gave a full-throated endorsement of the ad, calling it “pay dirt” and eviscerating DeWine for speaking out against it, calling him “disloyal.”

“Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!” Trump wrote on social media.

Yesterday, Vance, a former Ohio senator, said he was “disgusted” by Republicans for “whining” about the advertisement.

Ramaswamy, 41, ran for president in 2024 as a critic of “woke” and an acolyte of Trump. A former start-up executive, he was briefly involved with Elon Musk’s DOGE effort before he launched a run for governor of Ohio last year.

His bombastic and internet-savvy political style has always been an awkward fit with the Republican establishment there, and the bust-up over the ad has brought those tensions to the fore.

Campbell Robertson, a reporter on The Times’s National Desk who covers Ohio, told me that Ramaswamy is part of a larger shift in the state’s politics. Not everyone in the state had been comfortable with the change — and that was before the ad.

The archetypal Republican in Ohio used to be DeWine, who has served in every conceivable public post, from county prosecutor to U.S. senator, and finally, governor. Now, that mold is broken.

You had Vance, who came out of the private sector with no electoral experience in 2022. Then Bernie Moreno, who pushed that model a little further in 2024. And Ramaswamy was pushing it even further.

Until now, Campbell said, the establishment largely kept quiet about Ramaswamy. This ad has changed that.

Other Ohio Republicans to denounce the ad include Frank LaRose, the secretary of state; Lydia Mihalik, director of the Department of Development; a former governor, John Kasich; and a former senator, Rob Portman. Ramaswamy’s far-right opponent in the primary, Casey Putsch, also slammed the ad.

Even Senator Jon Husted, a Trump favorite who is running in a tight race to keep his seat, said: “I would not have run that ad.”

Get Caught Up

A covert Russian influence operation is spreading a fabricated claim of misconduct about James Talarico, the Democratic Senate candidate in Texas. Most of Russia’s election disinformation in this cycle has targeted Democrats.

A federal judge blocked the Homeland Security Department from carrying out most of its field operations focused on uncovering voter fraud in nine states, including California.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was in Maine today, where she held a town hall event with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate. Jackson said Ocasio-Cortez was “exactly what I want from my government — somebody that’s not afraid to stand up, fight for what she believes in.”

Trump is in Iowa to hold a rally with Ashley Hinson, the Republican Senate candidate, while Vance campaigned in Nebraska today for Senator Pete Ricketts.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the House Democratic leader, will be in New York’s Hudson Valley this weekend with Cait Conley. Conley, a combat veteran, is trying to unseat Representative Mike Lawler in one of the country’s most competitive districts.

The Justice Department is investigating Corey Lewandowski, who managed Trump’s first presidential campaign, over accusations that he profited from his role as a top adviser to the Homeland Security Department.

Calley Means, a leader of the Make America Healthy Again movement, has resigned from the Trump administration after growing frustrated with stalled progress on the MAHA agenda.

in one graphic

In 2024, young voters’ support for the Democratic Party was at its lowest point in two decades. Now, those 18-to-29-year-olds are returning to the party in sizable numbers.

Claire Cain Miller looked at data from the most recent New York Times/Siena University poll. A few of her takeaways:

The economy is the biggest factor for young people’s shift: 94 percent said economic conditions were either poor or fair, and 86 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of the economy.

The Iran war is also deeply unpopular, with 87 percent of young voters disapproving.

Young voters are increasingly worried about the country’s future. Fifty-three percent of those polled told us they feared the United States was in danger of failing as a nation. (Two years ago, that figure was 38 percent.)

Related: The Times crunched the numbers and found that, yes, life really has gotten more expensive over the past few decades — often far outpacing inflation.

Quote of the Day

That was Trump at a rally last night in Clemson, S.C., appearing to celebrate an attendee who had physically confronted a protester.

Protesters interrupted the rally at least a half dozen times, screaming and flipping him the middle finger. Rallygoers responded with aggression, often getting into altercations with the demonstrators.

Trump, for his part, did little to de-escalate the tense atmosphere. “They’re terrible people,” he said after another disruption.

Read more from Emily Davies, who was there.

Debate Takeaways

There were debates last night in the closely contested Senate races in Michigan and Kansas, and one surprising word appeared in our recaps of both events: “civil.”

Mike Rogers, the Republican, made an appeal to Democratic voters who had not supported his opponent, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, during the primary — particularly Black and Jewish voters.

And El-Sayed tried something similar, pointing to the crowds he drew on a tour across Michigan’s conservative Upper Peninsula last week. Voters there, he said, brought up the same concerns about costs as people he had met elsewhere in the state.

Read more Michigan takeaways.

Roger Marshall, the Republican, worked to connect his opponent, Adam Hamilton, to the broader Democratic Party. Marshall repeatedly invoked Chuck Schumer, the Senate Democratic leader, and said Hamilton would be beholden to him. Hamilton, for his part, tried to keep his distance, describing Joe Biden’s immigration policy as a “disaster.”

Marshall did not take the same tack with his own party. He said Trump had strengthened the nation’s military, secured the borders and passed a sweeping tax cut.

Read more Kansas takeaways.

ONE LAST THING

I ate this plate of lightly fried chicken tenders earlier this month, while I was out reporting on a Senate candidate whose grandfather claimed to have invented the dish. Which candidate is that?

Roger Marshall, Kansas Republican

Chris Pappas, New Hampshire Democrat

Ashley Hinson, Iowa Republican

Dan Osborn, Nebraska independent

Click an answer, and it’ll take you to my latest story so you can see if you were right. We’ve made the link free to read.

Taylor Robinson contributed to this newsletter.
